origin.said:
# Icon Browser + Icon Manager (Brett, voice)

## 1. Icon Browser plugin
- Ship a starter library: download a couple thousand icons (open-licensed sets), stored as assets.
- Views: tree, grid, list, etc. Categorized, sortable, filterable, searchable. Tree thumbnails toggle on/off.
- Sources (configurable, any type): FTP/SFTP (credentials + root folder), MCP, REST API, HTTP/online, local folder, Google Drive folder, Google Photos album, Dropbox, etc. Per-type config form: credentials when needed, root/path, auth. 'Online' shows a big list of known icon repositories, each with a section for what's needed to access it (API key etc.). Secrets in the secure store.
- Packs: create icon packs by drag and drop between panes. Panes are collapsible and floatable.
- Tab groups: open one or many selected icons into a floating tab group, a docked tab group, or a pane. 'Open new tab group' spawns docked or floating; with a selection it holds those icons, empty it shows a + to add. Drag icons from tree to groups and group to group.
- Save a pack as an icon-pack asset.

## 2. Icon Manager
- Every UI and plugin gets an icon map (icon slots/tags -> icon). All of AmberX, Console, axHub, everything.
- List/grid of every UI with an icon map, filterable by app. Open a map, or open a live preview of the UI and drag icons onto the preview. Save / Apply makes it permanent for that icon tag.
- Global icon pack asset listing every icon in the whole system.
- Inheritance: assign a pack to the whole app (root), or per UI, or per plugin. The child overrides the parent.
- Save changes as a new pack: root/global pack, or a UI/plugin-scoped pack.
- Icon packs are separate from design/style packs. A design pack MAY reference an icon pack but does not have to.
- Switch packs globally; a randomize button reshuffles the whole icon set; generate cohesive packs that follow one theme/style.

## Rules
- Everything is registry assets, with API/MCP/CLI parity and voice control.
- Settings in categorized collapsible sections.
- Submit UI options to UI Review first (at least 3).

steps.text: Contracts: icon-map@1 (slots -> icon refs, scope app | ui | plugin, extends, inheritance child over parent) and icon-source@1 (kind, config, secretRef) asset types in asset-types.json; iconmap-rules.mjs + .d.mts (normalize, errors, ref parsing name | pack:<id>/<glyph>, resolve chain, randomize, cohesive generation), engine iconmap.ts exported from core; fixture spec/fixtures/icon-map.json + check-icon-map.mts; starter assets; validate --framework and schemas green; Kotlin twin recorded as deferred in PORTING.md
steps.why: new shared asset types + cross-port contract

steps.text: Icon library: framework/cli/icon-import.mjs (SVG -> icon-pack glyphs: path, circle, ellipse, rect, line, polyline, polygon; 24 grid; <= 600 glyphs per pack, sets split by category) downloads open-licensed sets (Lucide ISC, Tabler MIT, Feather MIT, Heroicons MIT, Bootstrap Icons MIT, Phosphor MIT) from npm into framework/icon-library/ (icon-library@1 index.json: sets -> packs, licence, counts, categories, tags), every pack a valid icon-pack@1; `icon-import.mjs library --check` (valid, in sync, size budget) wired into CI
steps.why: library format + converter correctness is a contract every port reads

steps.text: Runtime: rt.iconFor(name, scope) resolves through the icon maps (plugin / UI map -> app root map -> active icon pack -> framework glyph), React IconScope context, Icon.tsx reads it; settings keys axf.icons.* (map picks per scope, slot overrides) count as appearance settings so the hub look carries them to every app; actions icons.set | icons.apply | icons.pack | icons.randomize | icons.generate | icons.reset registered for voice / MCP / CLI; check-icon-map covers the runtime path
steps.why: cross-app GUI behaviour in the runtime + appearance contract

steps.text: Icon Browser plugin core (apps/console-web/plugins/icon-browser): plugin.json (lifecycle, commands block, help.json, builtWith), server part (library index + search from framework/icon-library, sources CRUD, private secret store in the data dir, packs save as icon-pack assets, maps list), web: page head, tree / grid / list views with categories, sort, filter, search, thumbnails toggle, virtualised grid; menu.ts entries; settings tab in categorized collapsible sections
steps.why: first consumer of the icon-library and icon-map contracts; shapes the plugin's data model

steps.text: Panes, packs and tab groups: collapsible / floatable panes (library, pack composer, details) on the dock engine; drag icons between panes to compose a pack; Save pack as an icon-pack asset (server writes it, runtime registers it); open one or many selected icons into a docked or floating tab group or a pane through WindowManager (openGroup / openFloating / addTab); 'Open new tab group' docked or floating, empty shows a + to add; drag tree -> group and group -> group
steps.why: changes how GUIs work across apps (window / dock engine use, drag-drop between hosts)

steps.text: Icon Manager page: list / grid of every UI with an icon map (console, plugins, axHub web, AmberX, Molly), filterable by app; map editor (slot -> icon, drops from the browser); live preview of the UI with drops onto its icons; Save / Apply makes the pick permanent for that slot; inheritance view (root -> UI -> plugin, child overrides); assign a pack at root, UI or plugin; Save changes as a new root / scoped pack; global 'every icon' pack; switch packs globally; Randomize; Generate cohesive pack (one set / style)
steps.why: cross-app GUI behaviour: icon maps for every app

steps.text: Sources: per-type config forms (local folder, HTTP, REST, MCP, FTP / SFTP, Google Drive, Google Photos, Dropbox, online repository) with credentials, root / path and auth; secrets saved to the plugin's private store by reference only; framework/schemas/icon-repos.json: the known online icon repositories with what each needs (API key, token, none) shown per repository; test connection; import from a source into the library
steps.why: forms and integrations on top of the contracts

steps.text: Icon maps for every app: framework/cli/icon-map.mjs scan | list | check scans the icon names each UI and plugin uses (console, plugins, axHub web, AmberX, Molly) and writes / updates their icon-map assets; CI check that no UI is without a map; MCP / CLI parity of the plugin commands checked (plugin-commands.mjs check)
steps.why: scanner + CI wiring

steps.text: Polish: help.json for every control, menu-reach, help-coverage, check-theme / check-controls / check-chrome-assets / plugin-lifecycle / plugin-pages green; settings sections finished; console re-bake
steps.why: conformance

steps.text: Screenshots (desktop + phone) of at least 3 UI options for the browser and the manager submitted to UI Review; report _claude/builds/reports/icon-browser-manager.md; THREADS.md; PR opened and linked
steps.why: review + hand-off

origin.brief:
# Postgres: ONE true location for all data sets, in its own container (Brett, Nov 7)

Orchestrator build id: `postgres-console` (profile all, 7 steps) with Plan Studio plan `postgres-for-the-console-orchestrator-id-registr-anyx` — read both (`node apps/console-web/plugins/build-orchestrator/orchestrator.mjs brief postgres-console`) and follow them, with this change: Postgres runs in its OWN Docker container, not inside the console's.

Problem: the same data lives in 3+ places (builds store, per-profile orchestrator files, pending list, journal, plans, tracker/catalog, feature-ledger, origins) read by different tools, constantly out of sync.

1. Contract (Fable): schema for builds, steps, plans, blueprints, journal, queue, accounts/workers usage, Shipped features, origins, ID registry (orchestrator assigns every id). Migrations versioned.
2. Own container: `axf-postgres` (official image, pinned), internal Docker network only (no public port), named data volume, healthcheck, restart policy, nightly backup + restore script, credentials in the vault/env (never in git). Compose/deploy files + docs.
3. Importer: every existing JSON source loaded losslessly, counts/hashes verified, duplicates resolved with a report.
4. Switch every reader/writer (orchestrator, Build manager, Builds page, Plan Studio, builds-live, merge queue, MCP/CLI, AmberX, axHub) to the DB. JSON files become generated read-only exports for git/sessions. Kill file locks.
5. CI check: no code writes those JSON files directly anymore.
6. Tests + perf check. Add to Shipped features.

Deploying the container is a VPS write: prepare it, and leave a one-command deploy for Brett/orchestrator. Progress: append `<time> START|DONE <step>` to PROGRESS.md here at each step; don't stop between steps. Commit, don't push.

steps.text: Schema + contract: builds, steps, plans, plan steps, IDs registry, pending ids, changes, journal, queue, origins, token log
Migration design: import every JSON file losslessly, dual-write period, rollback, JSON exports stay generated read-only for git/claude-sync
Bundle Postgres into the console container with data on a persistent volume (survives redeploys), backups
Orchestrator is the ID registry: planner requests IDs, orchestrator assigns + registers build ID and pending ID
Switch readers/writers over (Build manager, orchestrator, Plan Studio, to-do sync, Codebase changes, MCP/CLI); kill file locks, use transactions
Query screen in the console (read-only queries, saved queries)
Tests, perf check, docs

before.title: Patches/AmberX redesign: 8 game-style PREVIEWS for UI Review (no build until pick)
before.detail: Rebuild the entire AmberX UI (app and console) from scratch, ignoring the current look. Overall direction: make it look really good, like a polished Windows PC game UI — game-launcher / game-menu feel, rich depth, glow, motion, HUD-style panels, bold typography. Produce 8 distinct concepts within that game direction, each with its own style, colour theme and layout (e.g. sci-fi HUD, fantasy RPG menu, cyberpunk neon, racing/sports dashboard, tactical military, sleek AAA launcher, retro arcade, space strategy), and post each to UI Review so Brett can pick one. Reference: the Gizmo chat restyle from October. Brett's words: "The entirety of, of AmberX. Rewrite, rebuild the whole thing. Use its own style, its own design, its own color theme, its own layout. Just build that shit from scratch. Give me a whole shitload of fucking UI reviews to pick from, man." and "Make it look good, give it a really good, like a Windows game."

notes.text: Every concept must look and feel like a real, working desktop application, not a mockup or static screenshot: real navigation, working screens, real controls and states, using AmberX's actual features and data. Brett: "I love the design to look like a real application, dude."

PREVIEWS FIRST. Each of the 8 steps now only produces a preview (static mockup screens of what Patches / AmberX would closely look like in that style) and posts it to UI Review. Do NOT build any real app code. Stop after all 8 previews and wait for Brett to pick one in UI Review; only the picked concept gets fully built. Note: patches.amberxai.com (the Patches app) was deleted; the picked concept becomes its from-scratch rebuild. Brett: "before you go crazy building, I need some previews in the UI review. Okay, what it closely might look like."

ARCHITECTURE for the real build (after Brett picks a preview): compile Patches, AmberX, the Dev Console and axHub controls into ONE app with one look and one login. Front end: a game-launcher style home hub with a tile per module (AmberX, Console, Builds, UI Review, etc.) plus a sidebar to jump between them. Modular and stable: each module is its own service/container on the VPS with axHub as the gateway, so one module can crash, restart or be rebuilt without taking down the rest. Every module gets a health check and auto-restart; code for each module lives in its own folder on GitHub with nightly backups so nothing is lost again. MODELS: the orchestrator picks the model for every step; ignore the Opus set on the steps. Brett: "I want to do all those things but yeah the orchestrator is supposed to pick the model"

before.title: Universal voice + API control (everything controllable)
before.detail: Every setting, every screen and every button in the whole app (console, axHub, patches, AmberX, everything) must be fully controllable by the API and by voice. Everything is already an asset and a token, so build one control registry: each control gets a stable ID, type, allowed actions and a description; the API can list, find and act on any of them; voice maps spoken commands onto those API calls. Separate build so it can run in parallel with the others.

notes.text: Overlap (Nov 8 2026, ui-api-parity-rule): s6 is done by api-coverage@1 + ui-api@1 (CI). s2 and s4 are largely done by full-api-control (control@1 console.values / console.elements / console.actions over MCP+CLI); the per-plugin named-op work is split into ui-api-parity-{builds,agents,console,look,media,framework}. Re-scope before building: what is left is s3 (axHub web + AmberX controls) and s5 (voice layer).
Reconciler: paused: no live session or process runs it (worktree kept); was running

Auto-register every console screen, setting and button
Auto-register axHub, patches and AmberX controls
Generic API: list, search, get and act on any registered control
Voice layer: spoken command -> registry lookup -> API call, with confirmation for destructive actions
Coverage check: flag any UI element that isn't registered + end-to-end test

before.title: Slot-aware plan optimizer (pre-launch)
before.detail: Before the orchestrator launches a plan from the queue, it checks how many parallel sessions are enabled and how many slots are open, then optimizes/refactors the plan to use all available slots: build a dependency graph of the steps, group independent steps into parallel tracks (one per free slot), keep dependent steps in order, and give each track its own brief. Re-check slots at launch time; if slots change, re-balance.

steps.text: Read enabled parallel sessions and currently open slots at launch time
Late account binding: no account or session assigned in pending/queue; when the plan's turn comes up, count free slots on every Claude account and assign tracks across all accounts to fill every slot
Step dependency graph for a plan (which steps can run independently)
File ownership: each parallel track owns its own files; steps only run in parallel when their files don't overlap; lock shared files (configs) so sessions don't step on each other
Optimizer: split independent steps into N parallel tracks to fill free slots
Generate a separate brief per track; merge/progress markers per track
Rebalance when slots open or close mid-build + end-to-end test

Model-aware slots: when scanning accounts/slots, also read which models each account has available (Fable limit hit or not); Fable steps only go to accounts with Fable available; if no Fable anywhere, only Opus runs

before.title: Orchestrator checks Shipped features before splitting any job
before.detail: When the orchestrator receives a job and splits it into steps, it first checks the Shipped features ledger (which must hold every feature the orchestrator has ever built). It must: not build anything twice; not break or redo anything already done; and if a step would conflict with or change something already built, notify Brett (AmberX notification) and wait before going on. Make the Shipped features ledger complete (backfill every landed build) and keep it updated on every land. Also standing rule: ONLY the orchestrator launches builds, picks model and account, owns pending/queue and monitors status; voice/chat sessions only hand it requests.

notes.text: Conflict flow (Brett): a conflicting step is moved to a special Conflicts section and removed from the build; the other steps still build. Brett gets an AmberX notification-panel item that explains the conflict and offers suggested resolutions; he taps a suggestion or types a prompt, which goes to the orchestrator, and the orchestrator makes a new build from it. Then test it: Brett will send a 3-4 step build that deliberately overlaps existing shipped features to confirm the orchestrator catches it.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Brett (Nov 9): "needs a way to go through all the pending builds and the build queue and search for steps that are gonna break existing work or conflict with it, or it's already done, or it doesn't need it anymore." Add a Sweep: a button on the builds page (and API/voice: 'sweep the builds') plus an automatic run on every land. It checks every step of every pending and queued build against the Shipped features ledger, main's code, and the other pending/queued builds, and flags each step: Already done (shipped by build X), Conflicts (would change/break feature Y, shows the files and lines), Duplicate (same as a step in build Z), Obsolete (no longer needed: superseded or its target was removed), OK. Results: badges on each build and step, a Sweep report with a filter per flag, and one-tap fixes per flag: drop step, merge into the other build, move to Conflicts for Brett, keep. Nothing is changed without Brett's tap. Cheap first pass in plain code (ledger + file overlap); Claude only for the unclear ones.

Correction (Brett): the Sweep does NOT run automatically on every land. It runs only (1) when Brett runs it (button / API / voice), and (2) by the orchestrator on a single build at two points: when it receives the job, and again right before it dispatches it (launches the session). Flags found at dispatch hold the build for Brett instead of launching.

Merged with orchestrator-checks-each-build-against-main-righ for the 'never build twice' part: every build is now checked against main (Shipped features, its PR, its branch, the files its steps create) right before it is queued and again at dispatch; done = closed, partly done = only what is left is queued. Still open here: the check at split time, the AmberX conflict notice and the ledger backfill.

before.title: UI = API parity: builds, plans and orchestration screens
before.detail: Part of the "every UI is fully API-controllable" rule (ui-api@1; build ui-api-parity-rule, which did the Demonstration Designer and Book Builder and the CI check). 437 gaps across 13 UI area(s) today (framework/spec/ui-parity-baseline.json). Per area: `node framework/cli/ui-parity.mjs gaps <area>`, then map each view/dialog in its plugin.json `ui` block (open = deep link, state = read command or value:<key>, actions = commands / console actions / settings, uiOnly with why), add any op that is missing, and `ui-parity.mjs write-baseline` once it went down. Model of a full map: apps/console-web/plugins/glossary-index/plugin.json `ui`. Audit: _claude/builds/reports/ui-api-parity-rule/audit.md.

notes.text: Clash: orchestrator-full-api-control (pending) adds step hold/resume/kill to the Build orchestrator; build them together so its controls are mapped once.

origin.said:
Standing rule: anything with a UI must have API functions that can do everything the UI can (open, read state, every action, every setting). Voice control is the app's main selling point and rides on this.

1. Orchestrator: every brief it writes for a build that touches UI includes this requirement explicitly (brief template + brief writer). Keep it short.
2. CI check: every registered UI asset/control/plugin view maps to API operations covering its actions and settings; fail when missing; report gaps.
3. Audit: list every existing UI lacking full API coverage, starting with the glossary/index Demonstration Designer and Book Builder; fix those two here, add the rest as pending builds.
4. Deep link per plugin view (URL that opens it) so agents can open any UI on the phone.

origin.said: AmberX notification panel (Brett): A real notification panel inside the AmberX phone app that receives every kind of notification and status from the console, orchestrator, axHub and builds. 1. Typed notifications: build started/done/failed, approvals and veto holds (with Deny / Run now), account status (checks starting/done, expired, limit, no credits), UI Review items, alerts, info. Extensible type registry. 2. Panel: list grouped by type/source, filters, unread counts, search, mark read, clear, pin; tap opens the related screen; action buttons per type. 3. Live status area: current account statuses, running builds, queue. 4. Also delivered as Android push notifications with actions; panel keeps history. 5. One send API every plugin uses (console, orchestrator, axHub); reuse existing notifications/alert hub code (notifications-control-panel groups/triggers/actions) where it exists. Rules: Full API + voice + MCP/CLI control; settings in categorized collapsible sections (per-type on/off, sound, priority); 3 UI options to UI Review; phone screenshots; tests; report, STATUS, THREADS.

before.title: Slot watchdog crew member (Slot Warden)
before.detail: Plain-code watchdog (zero tokens) on the headless build slots and queue: every ~30 s checks each running slot against reality (tmux alive, claude pid alive, log advancing); dead / finished / hung -> release slot, mark build failed with reason (auth, limit, crash, hung), tell the orchestrator, notify Brett (type slot). Live status + intervention log in console and AmberX. Root fix: claude-headless.sh always releases its slot when Claude exits. Duplicate guard on launch and in the watchdog (reuses orchestrator-dup-check). Crew member Slot Warden on the roster.

origin.said:
Assign a crew member (agent profile in the roster, e.g. a 'Slot Warden') whose only job is watching the headless build slots and queue, all the time, in plain code (zero tokens).

1. Every ~30 s: check each running slot in framework/cli/agent-slots.mjs against reality (tmux session alive, claude -p pid alive, log advancing). Today 3 builds died in 1-3 s on bad logins but kept all 3 slots, freezing the queue.
2. Dead / finished / hung (no log progress past a threshold) -> release the slot, mark the build failed with the reason (auth, limit, crash, hung), tell the orchestrator so it can relaunch/fail over (account-health-failover build), and notify Brett's phone (AmberX notification panel, type 'slot').
3. Report: a live slot/queue status the console and AmberX show; a log of every intervention.
4. Also fix the root: claude-headless.sh must always finish/release its slot when Claude exits, even on instant auth failure.

Duplicate guard (Brett): The watchdog and the launcher refuse or stop duplicate builds: same brief/goal running twice (e.g. memory-manager-r2 and -r3 both ran). On launch, compare against running + queued builds (name stem, brief source, build id); keep the furthest-along one, stop/dequeue the other, tell the orchestrator and notify Brett. Reuse the unlanded orchestrator-dup-check branch.

before.title: Agent profile schema: skills + personas, with a big template library
before.detail: Contract work (Fable). New asset schemas for crew agents: agent-skill@1 (name, domain, what it does, tools allowed, files/areas it owns, rules, checks it runs, model preference, cost cap, examples) and agent-persona@1 (name, nickname, voice/tone, job title, avatar, how it reports, strengths, limits), plus agent-profile@1 that combines one persona with several skills. Validators, fixtures, CI check. Ship a large library of boilerplate templates: skills (React UI, Kotlin/Compose, Python server, plugin manifests, themes/skins, tests, docs, merge-fixer, CI fixer, slot watchdog, account health, notifications, voice/API wiring, security review, UI Review designer, demo/pitch writer, data/Postgres, deploy/Coolify, refactor, perf) and personas (lander, reviewer, builder, watchdog, reporter, etc.). Template picker + 'new from template' in the Crew plugin; migrate the existing roster (Earl, Rhonda, Sully, Lenny, Gina, Paulie, Joey, Vinnie) onto it. Orchestrator reads skills when assigning steps. Every UI gets full API + voice + MCP/CLI control. Settings in categorized collapsible sections; 3 UI options to UI Review; tests; report.

before.title: Headless loop guards: stop endless loops and searches
before.detail: Guards on every headless session the orchestrator launches (claude-headless.sh + agent-slots + the running-builds watchdog's afterTick hook in pipeline.mjs): 1) Hard caps per session: --max-turns, wall time and cost cap derived from the step estimates (e.g. 2x estimate), settings with defaults. 2) Step progress timer: no step tick within 1.5x the step's estimate -> warn note, at 2x -> stop the session, build back to pending with the reason. 3) Loop detector reading the live log: the same command/tool call (or near-identical grep/find/sed) repeated N times, or M searches in a row with no edit/commit -> stop and note. 4) Search budget per step (e.g. 15 greps/finds) written into the brief and enforced by the detector. 5) Every stop: build note with the reason and last log lines, AmberX notification (normal notification, not an alarm), slot released, no auto-relaunch of a looped step until Brett says. 6) Brief line: 'If you can't find something in 3 searches, stop and leave a note.' Settings in orchestrator settings (categorized sections), full API/MCP/CLI/voice control. Tests with fake logs: repeated command, search spree, no tick, cost cap.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control and a deep link. Stock controls, 3 layout options to UI Review.

Brett on managing the safeguards: "I don't want the file itself to be editable. I want it to be view. You can view the file with steps. Make it an MD file with bullet points for the rules. before.title: Shipped Features: live manifests from dispatch to done, badges + progress meter
before.detail: Builds on shipped-manifest-api (landed 79ed472c0f1f, shipped-manifest@1). Today the manifest is sent only when a build lands. Change: the orchestrator sends a manifest to Shipped Features (and Plan Studio, per the queued Plan Studio manifest build) at every event: when it dispatches the job, on every build update (model/account change, note, hold, guard stop), on every step completed, and on completion/land. Each manifest is versioned (sequence number, previous version kept as history) and validated. The Shipped Features entry exists from dispatch, not only after landing, and shows a live status badge (dispatched, building, step x/y, waiting on UI Review, held, stopped by guard, failed, landed, shipped) plus a progress meter (steps done / total, time and cost used vs estimate), updated in real time (live push, no refresh). History view per entry shows every manifest. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control and deep link. Tests: dispatch creates the entry, each step tick bumps the version and meter, land sets shipped; invalid manifest is refused with the reason.

notes.text: Brett: "it lists what files were touched too, but they're hidden... in a collapsible, in an expanded row... you gotta expand a few things to get to them. They'll open in a dialog, which also you can click the files and open in a read-only editor. Checkbox to make it editable." Each manifest lists the files touched (added/changed/deleted, per step). In Shipped Features they sit tucked away: entry row > expand > Details > collapsed 'Files touched' section (grouped by step and folder, counts). Clicking it opens a dialog with the file list; clicking a file opens it in a read-only code editor (syntax highlight, diff vs before toggle). A 'Make editable' checkbox in the editor switches it to edit mode; saving goes through a normal commit with Brett's name and a change entry, never silent. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Brett: "when you open the file, it will jump to the feature that you found it through and highlight it. In focus, centered in screen." The manifest records, per touched file, the line ranges each step/feature changed. Opening a file from a Shipped Features entry scrolls the editor to that feature's code, centers it on screen, and highlights the changed lines (theme highlight colour); if a feature touched several spots, next/previous buttons jump between them. Same when opened via API/deep link (file + feature + range).

Brett: "Any failed, any errors that are file related get sent to the log with links to the file with the bad code there, the conflicted code, and highlighted and in focus." Every file-related failure (test/typecheck/lint/CI errors, merge conflicts, guard stops, parse errors in JSON) is written to the terminal log and the Shipped Features entry's manifest with file path + line range + message. Each log line carries a link; clicking it opens the file in the read-only editor scrolled to the bad or conflicted code, centered and highlighted (conflicts show both sides). Same via API/deep link.

Brett: "also make an errors column that's hideable. With a collapse button." In the Terminal plugin (console-terminal), add an Errors column: a side column next to the output showing only the file-related errors (file, line, message, build, time; click opens the file at the bad code, centered and highlighted). It has a collapse button (collapses to a thin strip with an error count badge) and can be hidden entirely from the Terminal toolbar/settings; state remembered. Filters by build, severity, plugin. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control.

Brett: prompt field to jump into a headless session. A running claude -p can't take input, so: a prompt field (on the build's Shipped Features entry, the Errors column line, and the session window) that, on send, does NOT send right away: it opens a confirm dialog warning that the running session will be stopped and any unfinished, uncommitted work in progress may be lost, showing what's at risk (current step, uncommitted files count, time/cost so far). Only on Confirm: stop the session cleanly (let it commit if it can), then resume the SAME session (claude --resume <session id>) with Brett's prompt so its context is kept; logged as a build note and a manifest update. Cancel keeps the prompt as a draft. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control, with the same confirm step.

before.title: UI Roller: roll a random style on any UI element
before.detail: New UI Roller plugin (console, AmberX, Molly, axHub web; every app built on the framework). 1) Context menu on EVERY UI element (dialogs, windows, panels, bars, buttons, inputs, menus, text, widgets; all registry assets): 'Roll style' and, when the element has a roll, 'Reset element'. 2) 'Roll style' opens a dialog: checkboxes for what to roll (colours, typography, spacing/density, size, radius/shape, borders, shadows, motion, icons), optional scope (this element / all of its type / its plugin), live preview, Re-roll, Apply. Rolls stay within valid token ranges and keep contrast readable. Apply saves the result as asset token overrides (local-first, like other overrides). 3) Main Settings > Rolled assets page: lists every app and plugin with its rolled assets (tree, counts, filters, search); each shows a live preview of the asset and its roll; actions: Reset (one), Reset selected (multi-select), Reset all. Undo/history per roll. 4) Applying a skin, design pack or theme clears EVERY rolled asset: covered ones take the new look, all others go back to their defaults. 5) Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control and deep links for roll, reset, reset selected/all and the page. Stock framework controls; 3 layout options to UI Review; tests (roll writes tokens, reset restores, theme apply clears all rolls); report.

before.title: Skins are a complete rework: look + layout + behavior, and professional skins
before.detail: After skins-finish lands (skin@1 + skin-coverage@1 for every asset type). Today a skin covers look only; layout and behavior live in design packs. Change: a skin is the complete rework of an app. Extend skin@1 (contract, Fable) to carry everything a design pack does: look (colors, grid and hover/selection colors, typography sizes, spacing/density, radius, borders, shadows, icons, motion), layout (nav placement, app menu, toolbars, banners, panel arrangement, grid density) and behavior (how menus open/slide/collapse, context menu style, hover/press feedback, transitions, overflow rules) for every registry asset type: nav menu, app menu, context menu, grids, dialogs, windows, bars, widgets, text. Design packs fold into skins (migrate, keep a compatibility alias). Applying a skin swaps all of it at once and resets rolled assets (UI Roller rule). CI: every asset type has skin coverage for look, layout and behavior. Then design at least 5 complete professional skins (clean enterprise, dark pro, compact data, modern SaaS, plus one more), applied to the real console, AmberX and Molly; post each to UI Review with desktop and phone shots; the pick becomes the default. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control. Tests; report.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 17 steps (5 Fable).

origin.said: I want the skins to be everything. I want a skin to be a complete rework. Everything. The skins are gonna rewrite the navigation menu, the app menu, the context menu, all the colors in the grids, the hover colors, the text sizes. All the behavior, everything. I need the entire UI reworked to look professional.

steps.text: Extend the skin@1 contract so one skin carries everything a design pack does. Add three sections: look (colors, grid/hover/selection colors, typography sizes, spacing/density, radius, borders, shadows, icons, motion), layout (nav placement, app menu, toolbars, banners, panel arrangement, grid density) and behavior (menu open/slide/collapse, context menu style, hover/press feedback, transitions, overflow rules). Cover every registry asset type: nav menu, app menu, context menu, grids, dialogs, windows, bars, widgets, text. Extend skin-coverage@1 to track look, layout and behavior separately per asset type.
steps.why: Cross-port contract change to skin@1 and skin-coverage@1 that every app consumes

steps.text: Design the schema and migration that fold design packs into skins. Map each design-pack field to a skin@1 field, write a versioned migration for stored packs and user selections, and add a design-pack compatibility alias that resolves to the skin, with a deprecation note.
steps.why: Schema plus migration design across stored data and contracts

steps.text: Rework the skin apply engine so applying a skin swaps look, layout and behavior in one atomic step. Follow the UI Roller rule and reset rolled assets on apply. Roll back cleanly on failure and emit one skin-changed event that the console, AmberX and Molly all listen to.
steps.why: Engine internals that change how GUIs apply skins in every app

steps.text: Make the framework layout runtime skin-driven. Read nav placement, app menu, toolbars, banners, panel arrangement and grid density from the active skin instead of from design packs, with no per-app hardcoding.
steps.why: Changes how layout works across all apps

steps.text: Make the framework behavior runtime skin-driven. Menu open/slide/collapse, context menu style, hover/press feedback, transitions and overflow rules should all come from the active skin, for every asset type in the registry.
steps.why: Changes how GUI behavior works across all apps

steps.text: Add a CI check that fails unless every registry asset type has skin coverage for look, layout and behavior in every shipped skin. Wire it into the existing skin-coverage job.

Update the Skins plugin UI. Show look, layout and behavior per skin, add a live preview, add apply and reset-rolled actions, and show a migrated-from-design-pack badge. Remove or redirect the Design Packs UI to Skins through the compatibility alias. API part: add a deep link (console_open target skins and skins/<id>), make state readable (active skin, preview, coverage), and define the actions and settings, which the next step exposes.

Give skins full API control, the same across all four surfaces. Operations: list, get, preview, apply, reset rolled assets, set default, read coverage, and run the design-pack migration. Surfaces: REST routes on the console API, MCP tools as console actions and plugin commands, CLI subcommands, and AmberX voice intents. Add console_show / console_open targets.
Design the professional skin 'Clean Enterprise' with complete look, layout and behavior for every asset type.
Design the professional skin 'Dark Pro' with complete look, layout and behavior for every asset type.
Design the professional skin 'Compact Data': dense grids, tight spacing, data-first layout, with complete coverage for every asset type.
Design the professional skin 'Modern SaaS' with complete look, layout and behavior for every asset type.
Design the professional skin 'High Contrast Accessible' (WCAG AAA contrast, larger targets, reduced motion), with complete coverage for every asset type.
Apply all five skins to the real console, AmberX and Molly. Fix any spots that hardcode look, layout or behavior so they follow the skin instead.

Capture desktop and phone screenshots of each skin on the console, AmberX and Molly, then post each skin to UI Review. Wire it so the picked skin becomes the default. API part: make the default readable and settable through REST, MCP, CLI and voice.
Update the docs: skin@1 authoring guide (look, layout, behavior), design-pack migration and alias, and how to reach each skin feature through REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

Tests, report, THREADS row and PR. Tests cover: contract validation, migration plus alias, atomic apply plus rolled-asset reset, layout and behavior runtime, CI coverage, and API parity across REST, MCP, CLI and voice. Write _claude/builds/reports/skins-are-a-complete-rework-look-layout-behavior.md, add the THREADS row, and open the PR stating how each UI feature is reached by deep link, state read, actions and settings.

before.title: Reserve build IDs at once: add returns the ID with the veto countdown
before.detail: Today pending_change add (and control_add on planner.builds/plans) is held on the 90 s veto countdown and the orchestrator only assigns the build ID when it runs, so callers (Claude sessions) must guess the ID from the title to add notes. Fix: the orchestrator (ID registry) reserves the ID the moment the call arrives, before the hold, and returns it in the held result (e.g. reservedId). Notes, sub prompts and status calls on a reserved ID queue up and apply in order once the add runs; if Brett denies the add, the reservation and anything queued on it are dropped. IDs never collide (registry check). Same for plan_park and plan_add. Tests: add returns the id while held; a note on the reserved id lands after the add; deny drops both.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 8 steps (2 Fable).

origin.said: Why do you have to guess its ID? Why can't you get it? ... Yeah, of course.

steps.text: Design the reservation model in the orchestrator's ID registry. Add a `reserved` state with reservedAt, origin call, kind (build|plan) and holdId. Add a per-ID ordered queue of pending ops (note, sub prompt, status), each with a seq and a payload. Store it in _claude/builds/store.json and add a migration that leaves existing entries untouched. Write the registry API in pipeline-core.mjs: reserveId(title, kind) checks for collisions against live builds, plans, shipped and existing reservations; commitReservation(id) turns a reservation into a real build; dropReservation(id) removes it and its queue.
steps.why: Schema and migration design for the build ID registry, which every port's contract depends on

steps.text: Change the veto-hold contract so the ID is reserved before the hold starts. Held results carry reservedId, holdId and secondsLeft. On approve or timeout, commitReservation runs and then the queued ops are replayed in seq order. On deny, dropReservation runs. Write down the contract for every caller: pending_change add, control_add on planner.builds/plans, plan_park, plan_add.
steps.why: Cross-port contract change to the held-result shape that all callers rely on

steps.text: Wire pending_change add and control_add (planner.builds and planner.plans) through reserveId so the held result returns reservedId right away. Approve and deny on the hold call commit or drop the reservation.
Wire plan_park and plan_add the same way: reserve the ID before the hold, return reservedId in the held result, and commit or drop when the hold resolves.

Queue notes, sub prompts and status calls that target a reserved ID. The note, sub prompt and status handlers check whether the ID is reserved and, if so, add the op to the queue instead of failing. The queued result says queued:true with its seq. Replay applies the ops in order after the add runs.
Show the reserved ID and the queued op count on the veto countdown card in the console Build manager. Add a 'copy ID' action. Deep link: console_show target build-orchestrator/hold/<reservedId>.

API part for the reservation and countdown UI. REST: GET /api/builds/reservations and GET /api/builds/reservations/<id> read the state (status, secondsLeft, queued ops); POST approve and POST deny act on the hold. MCP: console actions builds.reservation.get, builds.reservation.approve and builds.reservation.deny, plus control@1 for planner items. CLI: axf builds reservation get|approve|deny <id>. AmberX voice intents for the same three actions. All four surfaces call the same handlers.

Tests, report and PR. Write tests for: add returns the ID while held; a note on the reserved ID lands after the add runs; deny drops the reservation and its queued note; no ID collision when two adds with the same title arrive together; plan_park and plan_add return reservedId; REST, MCP and CLI give the same results. Write _claude/builds/reports/reserve-build-ids-at-once-add-returns-the-id-wit.md. Add the THREADS row. Open the PR, stating how the reservation and countdown are reached through the deep link, REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

Write down the contract for every caller: pending_change add, control_add on planner.builds/plans, plan_park, plan_add.
steps.why: Cross-port contract change to the held-result shape that all callers rely on

steps.text: Wire pending_change add and control_add (planner.builds and planner.plans) through reserveId so the held result returns reservedId right away. Approve and deny on the hold call commit or drop the reservation.
Wire plan_park and plan_add the same way: reserve the ID before the hold, return reservedId in the held result, and commit or drop when the hold resolves.

Queue notes, sub prompts and status calls that target a reserved ID. The note, sub prompt and status handlers check whether the ID is reserved and, if so, add the op to the queue instead of failing. The queued result says queued:true with its seq. Replay applies the ops in order after the add runs.
Show the reserved ID and the queued op count on the veto countdown card in the console Build manager. Add a 'copy ID' action. Deep link: console_show target build-orchestrator/hold/<reservedId>.

API part for the reservation and countdown UI. REST: GET /api/builds/reservations and GET /api/builds/reservations/<id> read the state (status, secondsLeft, queued ops); POST approve and POST deny act on the hold. MCP: console actions builds.reservation.get, builds.reservation.approve and builds.reservation.deny, plus control@1 for planner items. CLI: axf builds reservation get|approve|deny <id>. AmberX voice intents for the same three actions. All four surfaces call the same handlers.

Tests, report and PR. Write tests for: add returns the ID while held; a note on the reserved ID lands after the add runs; deny drops the reservation and its queued note; no ID collision when two adds with the same title arrive together; plan_park and plan_add return reservedId; REST, MCP and CLI give the same results. Write _claude/builds/reports/reserve-build-ids-at-once-add-returns-the-id-wit.md. Add the THREADS row. Open the PR, stating how the reservation and countdown are reached through the deep link, REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

before.title: Permissions control panel: every axHub tool's policy in one place
before.detail: Repo: axHub (policy store) + console/axhub-web screen. One Permissions panel listing every connected service and every tool (vps.build_start, vps.run, axf-console.*, github, hostinger, amberx...) with its policy (allow / veto countdown / confirm / deny), countdown length, who may call it (Brett's sessions, Claude sessions, headless builds, agents), and passes. Brett changes a policy with a dropdown; bulk change per service or by filter (destructive, writes, reads). Tree grouped by service > category, search, filters, live type-ahead. Every change logged with history and undo. Claude sessions and builds can read policies but never change them (owner-only, enforced on the hub, not just the UI). First change: set vps.build_start to deny so only the orchestrator launches builds. Full API (read for all, write owner-only), voice for Brett. 3 layout options to UI Review.

notes.text: Brett: "Can I make it so that employees like Molly or Amber or Moses can use it, and then I assign one of the employees to the orchestrator so the orchestrator can say run it, change it?" Permissions are granted per employee (agent from the one roster: Molly, Amber, Moses, Brownie, etc.), not just per session type. Brett assigns an employee to the orchestrator; the orchestrator acts with that employee's permissions. Brett can grant an employee permission to change policies, but only within a ceiling Brett sets: an employee can never raise its own or another's permissions above the ceiling, never touch owner-only settings or the ceiling itself, every change it makes is logged with the employee's name and sends Brett a notification, and Brett can revoke instantly. Panel shows per-employee view and per-tool view.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 15 steps (2 Fable).

origin.said: I need a control panel for all those settings, those permission settings.

steps.text: Design the axHub policy store schema and migration. One record per tool (service, tool id, category tags destructive/writes/reads, mode allow|veto|confirm|deny, countdown seconds, allowed callers brett-session|claude-session|headless-build|agent, passes). Add an append-only change-history table with actor, before/after and undo link. Write a migration that imports today's scattered veto/confirm/pass settings into the store without changing any effective policy.
steps.why: Schema plus migration design for the hub's central policy store

steps.text: Define the cross-port policy contract axhub-policy@1. It covers REST shapes (tree, search, filter, get, set, bulk set, history, undo), MCP tool names, control@1 ops, the CLI verbs, the live change event stream, and owner-only write semantics with error codes. Every surface (console API, MCP, CLI, AmberX voice) maps 1:1 to it.
steps.why: Cross-port contract shared by hub, console, MCP, CLI and voice

steps.text: Build the tool registry inventory. Enumerate every connected service and tool (vps.build_start, vps.run, axf-console.*, github, hostinger, amberx, ...) from the hub's connection manifests. Classify each tool into a category and destructive/writes/reads, and seed missing tools with a safe default (confirm). Re-sync when a service connects or disconnects.

Enforce policies on the hub, not in the UI. The tool-call gate resolves caller identity (Brett session, Claude session, headless build, agent) and applies allow/veto countdown/confirm/deny plus the caller list and passes. Policy writes are owner-only: any non-owner caller gets 403 with a clear message. Reads stay open to all authenticated callers.

Add the history and undo service. Every single or bulk change is written as one history entry, with a bulk change grouped under one id. Undo restores the before-state, is itself logged, and is also owner-only. Each change emits a live event for the panel.

Add the REST routes: GET /policies (tree grouped by service > category, with q= type-ahead search and filters by mode/category/caller), GET /policies/:tool, PUT /policies/:tool, POST /policies/bulk (by service or by filter), GET /policies/history, POST /policies/history/:id/undo. Write routes go through owner-only enforcement. Proxy the routes through the console API.

Expose the same operations through MCP and the CLI. Add MCP console actions (policy.list/get/set/bulk/history/undo), control@1 ops for policy items, and CLI `axf policy list|get|set|bulk|history|undo` with the same filters. Writes from Claude sessions and builds are rejected by the hub.

Add AmberX voice intents for Brett. Read intents: 'what's the policy for vps.run', 'which tools are deny'. Write intents: 'set github writes to confirm', 'undo last permission change', 'open permissions'. Writes need the owner voice session and are spoken back before they apply.

Build the shared Permissions panel core in console/axhub-web. It includes the data hook on GET /policies with live events, the policy dropdown per tool, countdown and caller editors, pass list, bulk change bar (per service or current filter), live type-ahead search, filter chips (destructive/writes/reads, mode, caller), and a history drawer with undo. Register deep link console_show/console_open target 'permissions' (with optional tool= / service= / filter=). Make the panel state readable via the console state API.

Build layout option A: a collapsible tree (service > category > tool) with an inline dropdown per row and a sticky bulk bar. It reuses the core and adds no new actions. The deep link 'permissions?layout=a' and the state read come from the core.

Build layout option B (dense filterable table with column sort and multi-select) and layout option C (service cards with a per-service default and expandable tool lists). Both reuse the core. Add deep links 'permissions?layout=b|c'.
Submit the 3 layouts to UI Review with screenshots and deep links. Add a setting for the chosen layout, readable and settable through REST, MCP, CLI (`axf policy layout`) and voice.

Make the first change as owner through the API: set vps.build_start to deny for every caller except the orchestrator's build-launch identity (via a pass). Check that a Claude session and a headless build are refused and that the orchestrator still launches builds. Record the change in policy history.

Write tests covering: migration keeps effective policies unchanged; enforcement for every mode and caller; owner-only writes rejected for Claude sessions, builds and agents on REST, MCP, CLI and voice; bulk by service and by filter; history and undo; registry sync; type-ahead search and filters; deep link and state read for each layout.

Run the full test suites and fix any failures. Write the report _claude/builds/reports/permissions-control-panel-every-axhub-tool-s-pol.md (what was built, the vps.build_start change, how each UI part is reached via deep link, state read, REST, MCP, CLI and voice). Add the THREADS row and open the PR, with the same API access table in the PR description.

before.title: Session transcripts API: search what was said, find which session
before.detail: Builds on ui-review-notify-session-audio (landed Nov 7): sessions are recorded by AmberX's Audio Output Recorder (output-recorder plugin) and transcribed by the faster-whisper worker, transcripts saved on the hub, readable in the recorder page. Today output-recorder's plugin.json declares no transcript commands, so nothing outside the page can read them. Add full API (plugin-commands@1, so MCP/axHub, REST, CLI, voice come for free): list sessions with transcripts (date, length, linked Claude session, title); read one transcript (whole or a time range, with timestamps); search across all transcripts (words or phrase, date range, fuzzy), returning the matching session, timestamp, a few lines of context, and a deep link that opens the recorder page at that moment (and plays the audio there). Also a 'find the session where we talked about X' command that ranks sessions by match. Reachable from Claude chat/voice sessions through axHub so Claude or Gizmo can answer 'which session did we talk about this'. Read-only; respects the recorder's settings. Tests; report.

notes.text: Brett: "I can find that internally without AI, right?" Yes: all search is plain code with zero tokens (full-text index over the transcripts, phrase + fuzzy + date filters). Add a search box with live type-ahead results on the recorder page and in the console's Search everything, so Brett can find a session himself without any AI. Claude/Gizmo only call the same plain search through the API.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Brett: results pop up in a scrolling window. As Brett types in Search everything (or the recorder page), matching transcript snippets pop up live in a scrolling results window: each hit shows the session (date, title), timestamp and a few lines around the match with the words highlighted; infinite scroll, grouped by session, newest first with a sort switch. Tapping a hit opens the recorder at that moment and plays the audio. Plain search also drops filler phrases like 'find the session where', 'when we talked about' so a whole sentence still works, zero tokens.

Brett: "With the keywords in focus." In the scrolling results window each snippet is centered on the matched keywords, highlighted. Opening a hit scrolls the transcript so the keyword is centered on screen, highlighted and focused, with next/previous match buttons inside that session.

Brett: "there's a column on the left with all the hits. All the sessions that match: the session name and the type of thing we were talking about." Results window layout: left column lists every session with hits (session name, date, hit count, and a topic tag for what it was about, e.g. builds, skins, approvals, AmberX); tapping one shows its hits on the right, keywords centered and highlighted. Topic tags: from the linked Claude session's title and the builds it touched (plain code, zero tokens); optionally a cheap one-time tag per session after transcription, off by default.

Brett: "I want a RAG database made of all the transcripts." Build a RAG store over every transcript: chunk each transcript (with session, date, timestamps, speaker, topic tags), embed the chunks with a local embedding model on the VPS (no Claude tokens), store them in Postgres with pgvector (reuse the postgres-console container plan if it exists, else its own table), and index every new transcript automatically after transcription. Two ways in: 1) semantic search (meaning, not just exact words) in the same results window, mixed with the keyword hits; 2) 'Ask' (API/MCP/voice): Claude or Gizmo retrieve the top chunks and answer with the sessions and timestamps as sources, each linking to that moment. Share the store with the Agent Manager's RAG knowledge (agent-profile build) so employees can use it. Settings: on/off, re-index, what gets indexed. Tests: retrieval returns the right session for a paraphrased question.
Split by rules (Claude: claude not available: spawnSync claude ETIMEDOUT): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 11 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: I want the API to be able to access the transcript so I can tell you or I can tell Gizmo, you know, what session was it that we talked about this or that.

steps.text: Design the transcript index: a schema for per-session metadata (id, date, length, title, linked Claude session id) and timestamped segments that the hub transcripts map onto, plus a migration that backfills the index from transcripts already saved on the hub. Document the contract that the API commands return (session, segment, match with context and deep link).
steps.why: Schema + migration design and a cross-port contract that MCP, REST, CLI and voice all share

steps.text: Build a read-only transcript reader over the hub store. It lists sessions that have transcripts (date, length, linked Claude session, title) with paging and date filters, and reads one transcript either whole or for a start/end time range, with a timestamp on every segment.

Build search across all transcripts. It supports words, exact phrase, date range and fuzzy matching (typo-tolerant), and returns the matching session, timestamp, a few lines of context and a deep link. Add the find-session ranking, which scores each session by its matches (count, phrase proximity, recency) for 'the session where we talked about X'.

Enforce the recorder's settings in the reader and search: recording or transcription off, retention window, sessions excluded or marked private, and the hub read scope. Every path stays read-only with no writes or deletes, and blocked results are returned as clear errors.

Declare the transcript commands in output-recorder plugin.json under plugin-commands@1: transcripts.list, transcripts.read, transcripts.search, transcripts.find_session and recorder.page_state. Each gets a parameter schema and is wired to its handler, so axHub MCP, console REST, CLI and voice pick them up.

Recorder page deep link (UI change, with its API part in this same step). The page opens at ?session=<id>&t=<sec>&play=1, scrolls the transcript to that moment, seeks the audio and plays it. Register it as a console_show/console_open target. The page state (open session, position, playing) is readable through recorder.page_state, and the open, seek and play actions are callable without the UI over REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

Make sure the commands are exposed the same way on REST (console API routes) and the CLI (transcripts list/read/search/find-session with --from/--to/--fuzzy/--json). Help text and output include the deep link.

Expose the commands through axHub MCP for Claude chat and voice sessions and Gizmo. Add voice intents for 'which session did we talk about X', 'read what was said at …' and 'open that session'. The spoken answer gives the session title, date and timestamp, and offers to open the deep link.

Unit tests: reader time ranges and timestamps, phrase, word and fuzzy search, date filter, context lines, find_session ranking order, policy enforcement (disabled, retention, private, read-only), and the index backfill migration.

Parity and integration tests: the same query through REST, MCP, CLI and voice gives the same result. The deep link opens the recorder page at the timestamp and plays the audio, and recorder.page_state reflects it.

Run the full test suite and fix any failures. Write the report, add the THREADS row and open the PR. The PR describes how each feature is reached: deep link, state read, actions and settings via REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

before.title: AmberX floating toolbar (always on top): mic + approvals + build status
before.detail: AmberX Android app: a small floating toolbar (overlay bubble, draw over other apps) that stays on top everywhere. Main items: mic button (talk to Claude / hands-free toggle) and approvals (badge with count of waiting axHub approvals; tap to approve/deny in place). Also build status (running count, failures). Draggable, collapsible, snaps to edges; every piece an asset, styled from tokens, configurable in settings (items, size, opacity, position). before.title: Skins as packages of slices: every section its own asset, pick sections on apply, mix creates a new skin via dialog, drag-and-drop Skin Builder
before.detail: Upgrade the existing skins/appearance system and asset registry; don't build a parallel one. 1) DATA MODEL: a skin is only a package (manifest) referencing section assets. Every section (colours, layouts, design/visual styles, behaviour, and every other category a skin covers) is its own standalone asset with a name, preview, tags and source. Convert every existing skin into this form, with no monolithic skins left. 2) APPLY WITH PICKS: when you apply, enable or change a skin, a dialog lists its sections with checkboxes and previews. before.title: Landing tool takes long build names, and auto-fixes and retries failed lands
before.detail: vps.build_land, build_start, build_stop and build_clean reject names over 40 characters (^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,39}$), but the orchestrator makes build IDs up to about 50 characters (e.g. demo-designer-finish-phase-2-s2-s3-resuming-from, skins-restyle-everything-badges-banner-and-every-visual-element). 1) In the axHub vps service, raise the name limit to match the orchestrator's longest IDs (at least 80), keeping the same safe character set. 2) If the orchestrator ever makes an ID the tools can't take, it shortens it consistently (folder, branch, tmux) instead of failing. 3) When build_land fails for any fixable reason (stray files, stale locks, name format), it fixes it and retries automatically, logging to the fix log. Real code clashes go to a conflict-fix build automatically. 4) Tests with long names. Repos: axHub (vps service config) and AmberX-AXF (orchestrator).

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 9 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: Why, when it has a problem, when it gets rejected, aren't you just fixing it right away? I keep telling you over and over.

steps.text: Define the shared build-name contract used by both repos. Allowed names match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,79}$ (80 characters). Define one deterministic shortener: trim at a hyphen boundary, then append -<6-char hash of the full ID>, so the same long ID always maps to the same short name. The folder, branch and tmux session all use the short name. The orchestrator records long→short in its build record. Write the contract doc and the reference shortener module with its constants (max length, charset, hash length).
steps.why: Cross-port contract between the axHub vps service and the AmberX-AXF orchestrator

steps.text: axHub vps service: replace the hard-coded ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,39}$ in build_land, build_start, build_stop and build_clean with one shared constant from service config allowing up to 80 characters, with the same safe character set. Error messages state the limit and the offending length.

Orchestrator: route every place that makes a build ID, worktree folder, branch name or tmux session through build-name.mjs. When an ID exceeds the tools' limit, shorten it consistently instead of failing. Store long_id and short_id in the build record and journal. Lookups accept either form.
files: AmberX-AXF: apps/orchestrator/ (ID creation, worktree, branch, tmux spawn)

steps.text: Orchestrator: build_land failure classifier. Parse build_land errors into categories: stray_files (untracked or tmp files such as *.json.tmp-*), stale_lock (index.lock or a stale land lock with a dead PID), name_format (rejected name), code_conflict (real merge conflict) and unknown. Unit-testable pure function with fixtures from real failure output.

Orchestrator: auto-fix and retry loop around build_land. For each fixable category, apply the fixer: remove or commit stray tmp files after looking at them, clear stale locks only if the owning PID is dead, re-derive the short name for format rejects. Then retry, up to 3 attempts. Each attempt, fix and outcome is appended to the fix log. Land state (attempt, last error, fix applied) is readable through the existing console build API, MCP, CLI and voice status read.
files: AmberX-AXF: apps/console-web/ build status route/MCP/CLI land-state fields

steps.text: Orchestrator: on code_conflict, or when retries are used up on an unknown error, automatically queue a conflict-fix build. The queued build links to the parent build, the conflicting files and the failed land log. The parent build is marked waiting-on-fix in place of failed. Log it to the fix log.

axHub tests: build_land, build_start, build_stop and build_clean accept the 50 to 64 character real IDs (demo-designer-finish-phase-2-s2-s3-resuming-from, skins-restyle-everything-badges-banner-and-every-visual-element) and an exactly-80-character name. They reject 81 characters, uppercase, a leading hyphen, slashes and dots.

AmberX-AXF tests: the shortener is deterministic, stays within the limit, keeps the folder, branch and tmux names identical, and has no collisions across the existing shipped build IDs. The classifier fixtures pass. The auto-fix loop recovers from stray files, stale locks and name format errors and logs to the fix log. A code conflict queues a conflict-fix build. A full long-name start, land and clean path is checked end to end against a mock vps.

Run the full test suites in both repos. Write the report: what changed, the name contract, each auto-fix category, the API reach of land state (REST, MCP, CLI, voice) and the test results with before and after. Add the THREADS row. Open PRs in axHub and AmberX-AXF, cross-linked, axHub merged first.

before.title: Auto-land every build the moment it finishes, redeploy the console on every land, and backfill the 134 unlanded
before.detail: Plain code in the orchestrator dispatcher, no AI. 1) The moment a build's session finishes with its steps ticked and tests green, the orchestrator lands it straight away: clean sync files and stray logs, clear stale locks, merge origin/main, rerun the build's own tests, push to main. No waiting on a person or a later session. 2) UPDATE THE CONSOLE ON EVERY LAND: right after each push to main, trigger the console redeploy immediately (the same path as install-console.sh's auto-update, run now, not on the 5-minute timer), and rebuild any other app the change touched (AmberX web, axHub web, Molly and so on). Wait for it to come up healthy, then refresh open consoles. If the deploy fails, roll back to the last good image and queue a fix. 3) UI Review never blocks landing: screenshots and picks can follow after landing, and changes come as follow-up builds. 4) If main moved and tests fail after the merge, or there's a code clash, the orchestrator immediately queues a conflict-fix run on the same branch (top priority, any working account) and lands when green. It retries until it's on main. 5) Land in finish order, one at a time (a merge lock), so each lands on the newest main. Batch redeploys if several land within a minute. 6) Backfill now: land every finished-but-unlanded build (about 134), oldest first, skipping ones superseded or already on main, with conflict-fix runs where needed. 7) Each land and deploy shows in the Activity Monitor and fix log, with a phone FYI only for failures that need Brett. Tests with fake clashes and a fake failed deploy. Supersedes any auto-land pieces in other builds; don't duplicate.

Reconciled with enforce-the-merge-queue (Nov 10 2026, Brett: 'Everything needs to go into the merge queue so we can make one build out of it before we send it to CI'). Redeploy-on-land happens once per landed batch. Keep the backfill: it should open PRs into the queue, not push.
Split by Claude into 15 steps (2 Fable).

origin.said: You realize when you don't merge stuff right away you have to pull in main again, and tests are gonna fail. Why do you not just merge this as soon as it's done? ... Right, so when something lands, update the console. Period.

steps.text: Design the land pipeline contract inside the orchestrator dispatcher. Define the land-queue state machine (finished → queued → locked → cleaning → merging → testing → pushed → deploying → landed | conflict-fix | deploy-failed). Define a merge lock that lands builds one at a time in finish order. Add a land record schema to the build store (landedAt, mainSha, deployId, attempts, lastError) with a migration that also adds a 'landed' field to existing builds. Write it up in the orchestrator README.
steps.why: Engine internals plus a schema and migration that every later step and the backfill depend on

steps.text: Implement the land core as plain code with no AI. Under the merge lock: delete sync temp files (*.tmp-*) and stray logs (.axf-*.log, .axf-brief.md), clear stale locks, fetch and merge origin/main into the build branch, rerun the build's own tests from its brief/report, then push to main. Return a typed result: landed, clash or tests-failed.
steps.why: Core dispatcher engine path that every land and the backfill run through

steps.text: Wire auto-land into the session-finish handler in the dispatcher. When a build's session ends with all steps ticked and tests green, put it on the land queue straight away, in finish order. Make UI Review non-blocking: screenshots and picks get queued as follow-ups after landing, and changes become follow-up builds. Remove the gates that waited on a person or a later session.

Add conflict-fix runs. On a clash, or on tests failing after the merge, queue a conflict-fix session on the same branch at top priority on any working account, using a fixed prompt template. When it finishes green, put the build back on the land queue. Retry until it is on main, with backoff and an attempts counter in the land record.

Redeploy the console on every land. Pull the auto-update path out of install-console.sh into a callable redeploy script and run it right after each push to main, with no 5-minute timer. Batch redeploys when several lands happen within 60 s. Wait for the health check to pass, then send a refresh event to open consoles.

Rebuild the other apps a land touched. Map the changed paths to apps (AmberX web, axHub web, Molly, …) and rebuild and redeploy each one, with its own health wait. This uses the same batch window as the console redeploy.

Add deploy rollback. Keep a last-good image tag for each app. When a deploy fails or its health check times out, roll back to that tag, record deploy-failed in the land record, and queue a fix build that carries the deploy log.

Report every land and deploy. Emit Activity Monitor events and fix-log entries for queued, landed, conflict-fix, deployed, rolled back and failed. Send a phone FYI only for failures that need Brett: a rollback that also failed, or a build still not on main after N conflict-fix attempts.

Add a Land queue panel to the Activity Monitor UI. It shows the queue, the current lock holder, recent lands and deploys, and conflict-fix runs. It offers these actions: land now, retry, skip, roll back. It has these settings: auto-land on/off and the batch window in seconds.

Give the Land queue full API control, the same across all four surfaces. Deep link: console_show / console_open target 'activity-monitor/land'. State read: the queue, the lock and the land records. Actions: land now, retry, skip, roll back, start backfill. Settings: auto-land and batch window. Expose these through REST routes, MCP console actions and plugin commands, the axf CLI subcommands 'land' and 'deploy', and AmberX voice intents.

Implement the backfill command. List the finished-but-unlanded builds, oldest first. Skip any that are superseded (checked through supersedes links) or already on main (checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor or a patch-id match). Put the rest on the land queue, which uses conflict-fix runs where needed. Support a --dry-run report.

Remove the duplicate auto-land pieces. Find the auto-land and merge code in other builds and modules (including build-manager leftovers and the shipping unblock in the orchestrator) and point them at the new land pipeline. Mark the overlapping queued builds as superseded by this one.

Write tests for the land pipeline using temporary git repos. Cover: the merge lock and finish order, a fake code clash leading to a conflict-fix run, a fake test failure after the merge, redeploy batching within 60 s, a fake failed deploy leading to rollback and a fix build, backfill skipping superseded and already-on-main builds, and API parity across REST, MCP and CLI.

Start the backfill. Run it with --dry-run and save the list in the report, then start the real backfill of about 134 builds, oldest first. Watch the first lands and redeploys come up healthy in the Activity Monitor, and note what is still queued.

Final step. Run the full test suite. Write the report at _claude/builds/reports/auto-land-every-build-the-moment-it-finishes-red.md, covering the backfill status and how each feature is reached through deep link, REST, MCP, CLI and voice. Add the THREADS row, then open the PR with the API reach list.

before.title: Approval page: allow-all / deny-all for a set time, plus a veto countdown length setting
before.detail: axHub approval page settings: 1) Allow all approvals for the next 1 hour, 2 hours, or a custom duration / until a set time. 2) Deny all for a custom duration / until a set time. 3) A setting to change the veto countdown length (today fixed at 90 seconds). Show the active window and let it be cancelled early. Full API control.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 10 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: I need a settings on the approval page to allow all for the next hour or two hours or a custom field that I can enter, or deny all for a custom field. Until a certain time or amount of time. And where's the switch? A setting to control the time of the 90 seconds.

steps.text: Design the approval policy schema and migration: a 'window' record (mode allow|deny, starts_at, ends_at, created_by, source ui|rest|mcp|cli|voice, cancelled_at) and a 'veto_countdown_sec' setting (default 90, bounds 10–3600). Only one active window at a time; a new window replaces the old one. Write the migration so existing installs keep 90 s and have no window. Document the contract in the approvals schema doc.
steps.why: Schema + migration design for persisted approval policy shared by server, MCP, CLI and voice

steps.text: Engine: before an approval is queued, check the active window. In an allow window, auto-approve it; in a deny window, auto-deny it. Log every auto-decision with the window id. Expire windows lazily on read and with a timer so expiry clears without a restart. Replace the hard-coded 90 s veto countdown with the veto_countdown_sec setting, read when each countdown starts.

Policy service: setWindow({mode, duration|until}), cancelWindow(), getPolicy() returning the active window with remaining time, and get/set veto_countdown_sec. Validate inputs: until must be in the future, duration must be within 24 h unless forced, countdown must be within bounds. Emit change events so the UI and phone notifications update live.

REST routes: GET /api/approvals/policy, POST /api/approvals/policy/window ({mode:'allow'|'deny', minutes | until}), DELETE /api/approvals/policy/window, GET/PUT /api/approvals/policy/veto-countdown. Use the existing console auth and audit logging.

Approval page UI, settings section: 'Allow all for' with 1 h and 2 h presets, a custom duration field and an until-time picker; 'Deny all for' with a custom duration and an until-time picker; a 'Veto countdown' number field (seconds, defaults to 90) with a save button. Use the plugin framework components and call the REST routes from the previous step.

Approval page UI, active-window banner: show the mode (allow or deny), a live countdown to the end time and the end time itself, plus a 'Cancel now' button. Show the same badge in the axHub header while a window is active. Update live from the policy change events.

API part for the UI (deep links and state): register console_show / console_open targets approvals/settings, approvals/settings#window and approvals/settings#veto-countdown. Expose the policy state through console state read. Add MCP console actions approvals.policy.get, approvals.window.set, approvals.window.cancel, approvals.vetoCountdown.get and approvals.vetoCountdown.set, all backed by the same policy service.

CLI and voice: add `axf approvals allow --for 2h|--until 18:30`, `axf approvals deny --for 30m|--until …`, `axf approvals window cancel`, `axf approvals status` and `axf approvals veto-countdown [<sec>]`. Add AmberX voice intents with the same meanings, for example 'allow all approvals for two hours', 'deny all until 6 pm', 'cancel the approval window', 'set veto countdown to 60 seconds' and 'what's the approval window', each confirmed by voice. Both go through the REST API.

Tests: policy service (set, replace, expire and cancel a window; validation), engine auto-approve/deny inside a window and normal flow outside it, configurable countdown, REST routes, MCP actions, CLI parsing of durations and until times, and the voice intent parse. Add a UI test for the settings form and the banner cancel button.

Final: run the full test suite. Write the report _claude/builds/reports/approval-page-allow-all-deny-all-for-a-set-time.md, including an API table showing how each feature is reached through the deep link, state read, REST, MCP, CLI and voice. Add the THREADS row in _claude/THREADS.md. Open the PR, with the same per-feature API reach list in its description.
