before.detail: Amends the Project Manager build. Drag a build (or similar item) from one project and drop it on another project's tab or window. A dialog asks where it goes: Pending, Queued or Planned, showing that project's current queue, pending list and plans. If Queued, pick the position: first, second, third... or last. Full API control.

notes.text: Queued by console.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 9 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: Drag a build over to another tab or window with the other project and drop it, and a dialog asks if you want to drop into pending, queued or planned. If queued, it asks what spot in the queue, first, second, third or last, while listing the current queue, the current pending, the current plan.

steps.text: Define the cross-tab and cross-window drag-and-drop contract for console items. Add a shared MIME type (application/x-axf-item+json) and payload shape {kind, id, title, sourceProject, sourceList}. Add a drop-target registration API that project tabs and project windows use. Add BroadcastChannel hover and drop-accept feedback between windows of the same console origin. Document the contract.
steps.why: Cross-window drag contract changes how GUIs in every console app exchange items

steps.text: Add the server-side move operation to the Project Manager store. Move a build (or other movable item) from one project to another project's Pending, Queued (with a position: 1-based index or 'last') or Planned list. Validate the item kind and target, clamp the position, write atomically, and record the move in the journal.

Add the REST routes. GET /api/projects/:id/lists returns the current queue (in order), pending and plans for the drop dialog. POST /api/projects/:id/items/move takes {item, from, to: pending|queued|planned, position}. Wire both into the console API router.

Expose the same move and lists operations through every other API surface. Add MCP console actions and plugin commands (project_lists, project_move_item) and control@1 planner-item support for moves into Planned. Add the CLI subcommands 'projects lists <project>' and 'projects move <item> --to <project> --into pending|queued|planned [--position n|first|last]'. Add AmberX voice intents ('move build X to project Y, queue second').

Make build rows (and similar items) in the Project Manager draggable using the new contract. Register each project tab and each project window as a drop target, with hover highlighting and refusal of drops onto the item's own project.

Build the drop dialog. Show the target project's current queue (numbered), pending list and plans. Let the user choose Pending, Queued or Planned. If Queued, show a position picker (first, second, third… last) with a preview of where the item will land. Confirm calls POST /items/move; cancel leaves everything unchanged.

Add full API control for the drop dialog. Add a deep link through console_show / console_open target 'project-manager/move?item=<id>&to=<project>[&into=queued&position=n]' that opens the dialog prefilled. Make the dialog state (open, item, target project, choice, position) readable through REST and MCP. Make its actions (choose list, set position, confirm, cancel) callable through REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

Write the tests. Unit tests for the store move (each target, positions first, middle and last, out-of-range clamp, same-project refusal). Route tests. MCP, CLI and voice parity tests against the same fixture. A UI test of drag, drop, dialog and confirm across two tabs.

Run the full test suite and fix any failures. Write the report _claude/builds/reports/project-manager-add-on-drag-a-build-to-another-p.md. Add the THREADS row. Open the PR, stating how each feature is reached by deep link, REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

before.title: Projects: create a new project and move builds between projects; move every pending build older than 2 days into a new project
before.detail: 1) Add create-project (valid project manifest, its own builds, notes, data; per the multi-project setup where picking a project switches all data) and move-builds-between-projects, by UI and full API (no AI). 2) Then create a new project and move every Pending build created before 2026-11-08 out of the current project into it, with their notes, steps, branches and history intact; nothing deleted or archived. Builds from the last two days stay. Report the list moved.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Queued by console.
Split by Claude into 10 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: I don't want to archive. I want to move to another, you know how we set it up from multiple projects. Each one has its own builds, its own notes, all that. Make a new project, remove those from this project and move them to the new project.

steps.text: Design the project contract. Write the project manifest schema covering id, name, created, and the builds, notes and data roots. Define move-build semantics: a build's store entry, journal lines, notes, steps, branches, PR links, reports, shipped records and change entries all move together and keep their ids. Specify the order of operations so a move is atomic (write the target with tmp files, then remove from the source, roll back on failure) and how id collisions are handled. Confirm that a project switch already switches all build data, and write the contract to a doc.
steps.why: Cross-project data contract and schema design that every later step and app depends on

steps.text: Build the createProject core library. Validate the manifest against the schema, scaffold the project's own builds, notes and data folders, register it in the projects registry and the /projects hub sync, and refuse duplicate ids. It is a pure function with no AI. Add unit tests.

Build the moveBuilds core library, following the contract from step 1. before.title: Approval page: allow-all / deny-all for a set time, plus a veto countdown length setting
before.detail: axHub approval page settings: 1) Allow all approvals for the next 1 hour, 2 hours, or a custom duration / until a set time. 2) Deny all for a custom duration / until a set time. 3) A setting to change the veto countdown length (today fixed at 90 seconds). Show the active window and let it be cancelled early. Full API control.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 10 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: I need a settings on the approval page to allow all for the next hour or two hours or a custom field that I can enter, or deny all for a custom field. Until a certain time or amount of time. And where's the switch? A setting to control the time of the 90 seconds.

steps.text: Design the approval policy schema and migration: a 'window' record (mode allow|deny, starts_at, ends_at, created_by, source ui|rest|mcp|cli|voice, cancelled_at) and a 'veto_countdown_sec' setting (default 90, bounds 10–3600). Only one active window at a time; a new window replaces the old one. Write the migration so existing installs keep 90 s and have no window. Document the contract in the approvals schema doc.
steps.why: Schema + migration design for persisted approval policy shared by server, MCP, CLI and voice

steps.text: Engine: before an approval is queued, check the active window. In an allow window, auto-approve it; in a deny window, auto-deny it. Log every auto-decision with the window id. Expire windows lazily on read and with a timer so expiry clears without a restart. Replace the hard-coded 90 s veto countdown with the veto_countdown_sec setting, read when each countdown starts.

Policy service: setWindow({mode, duration|until}), cancelWindow(), getPolicy() returning the active window with remaining time, and get/set veto_countdown_sec. Validate inputs: until must be in the future, duration must be within 24 h unless forced, countdown must be within bounds. Emit change events so the UI and phone notifications update live.

REST routes: GET /api/approvals/policy, POST /api/approvals/policy/window ({mode:'allow'|'deny', minutes | until}), DELETE /api/approvals/policy/window, GET/PUT /api/approvals/policy/veto-countdown. Use the existing console auth and audit logging.

Approval page UI, settings section: 'Allow all for' with 1 h and 2 h presets, a custom duration field and an until-time picker; 'Deny all for' with a custom duration and an until-time picker; a 'Veto countdown' number field (seconds, defaults to 90) with a save button. Use the plugin framework components and call the REST routes from the previous step.

Approval page UI, active-window banner: show the mode (allow or deny), a live countdown to the end time and the end time itself, plus a 'Cancel now' button. Show the same badge in the axHub header while a window is active. Update live from the policy change events.

API part for the UI (deep links and state): register console_show / console_open targets approvals/settings, approvals/settings#window and approvals/settings#veto-countdown. Expose the policy state through console state read. Add MCP console actions approvals.policy.get, approvals.window.set, approvals.window.cancel, approvals.vetoCountdown.get and approvals.vetoCountdown.set, all backed by the same policy service.

CLI and voice: add `axf approvals allow --for 2h|--until 18:30`, `axf approvals deny --for 30m|--until …`, `axf approvals window cancel`, `axf approvals status` and `axf approvals veto-countdown [<sec>]`. Add AmberX voice intents with the same meanings, for example 'allow all approvals for two hours', 'deny all until 6 pm', 'cancel the approval window', 'set veto countdown to 60 seconds' and 'what's the approval window', each confirmed by voice. Both go through the REST API.

Tests: policy service (set, replace, expire and cancel a window; validation), engine auto-approve/deny inside a window and normal flow outside it, configurable countdown, REST routes, MCP actions, CLI parsing of durations and until times, and the voice intent parse. Add a UI test for the settings form and the banner cancel button.

Final: run the full test suite. Write the report _claude/builds/reports/approval-page-allow-all-deny-all-for-a-set-time.md, including an API table showing how each feature is reached through the deep link, state read, REST, MCP, CLI and voice. Add the THREADS row in _claude/THREADS.md. Open the PR, with the same per-feature API reach list in its description.

before.title: Auto-land every build the moment it finishes, redeploy the console on every land, and backfill the 134 unlanded
before.detail: Plain code in the orchestrator dispatcher, no AI. 1) The moment a build's session finishes with its steps ticked and tests green, the orchestrator lands it straight away: clean sync files and stray logs, clear stale locks, merge origin/main, rerun the build's own tests, push to main. No waiting on a person or a later session. 2) UPDATE THE CONSOLE ON EVERY LAND: right after each push to main, trigger the console redeploy immediately (the same path as install-console.sh's auto-update, run now, not on the 5-minute timer), and rebuild any other app the change touched (AmberX web, axHub web, Molly and so on). Wait for it to come up healthy, then refresh open consoles. If the deploy fails, roll back to the last good image and queue a fix. 3) UI Review never blocks landing: screenshots and picks can follow after landing, and changes come as follow-up builds. 4) If main moved and tests fail after the merge, or there's a code clash, the orchestrator immediately queues a conflict-fix run on the same branch (top priority, any working account) and lands when green. It retries until it's on main. 5) Land in finish order, one at a time (a merge lock), so each lands on the newest main. Batch redeploys if several land within a minute. 6) Backfill now: land every finished-but-unlanded build (about 134), oldest first, skipping ones superseded or already on main, with conflict-fix runs where needed. 7) Each land and deploy shows in the Activity Monitor and fix log, with a phone FYI only for failures that need Brett. Tests with fake clashes and a fake failed deploy. Supersedes any auto-land pieces in other builds; don't duplicate.

notes.text: Queued by console.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Reconciled with enforce-the-merge-queue (Nov 10 2026, Brett: 'Everything needs to go into the merge queue so we can make one build out of it before we send it to CI'). Step 1 must not push to main: a finished build gets its PR and joins the merge queue (push-banner land/merge-queue.mjs enlist does this every 3 min already); the queue batches the ready PRs into one build on queue/batch, runs CI once and lands it on main as one commit. Redeploy-on-land happens once per landed batch. Keep the backfill: it should open PRs into the queue, not push.
Split by Claude into 15 steps (2 Fable).

origin.said: You realize when you don't merge stuff right away you have to pull in main again, and tests are gonna fail. Why do you not just merge this as soon as it's done? ... Right, so when something lands, update the console. Period.

steps.text: Design the land pipeline contract inside the orchestrator dispatcher. Define the land-queue state machine (finished → queued → locked → cleaning → merging → testing → pushed → deploying → landed | conflict-fix | deploy-failed). Define a merge lock that lands builds one at a time in finish order. Add a land record schema to the build store (landedAt, mainSha, deployId, attempts, lastError) with a migration that also adds a 'landed' field to existing builds. Write it up in the orchestrator README.
steps.why: Engine internals plus a schema and migration that every later step and the backfill depend on

steps.text: Implement the land core as plain code with no AI. Under the merge lock: delete sync temp files (*.tmp-*) and stray logs (.axf-*.log, .axf-brief.md), clear stale locks, fetch and merge origin/main into the build branch, rerun the build's own tests from its brief/report, then push to main. Return a typed result: landed, clash or tests-failed.
steps.why: Core dispatcher engine path that every land and the backfill run through

steps.text: Wire auto-land into the session-finish handler in the dispatcher. When a build's session ends with all steps ticked and tests green, put it on the land queue straight away, in finish order. Make UI Review non-blocking: screenshots and picks get queued as follow-ups after landing, and changes become follow-up builds. Remove the gates that waited on a person or a later session.

Add conflict-fix runs. On a clash, or on tests failing after the merge, queue a conflict-fix session on the same branch at top priority on any working account, using a fixed prompt template. When it finishes green, put the build back on the land queue. Retry until it is on main, with backoff and an attempts counter in the land record.

Redeploy the console on every land. Pull the auto-update path out of install-console.sh into a callable redeploy script and run it right after each push to main, with no 5-minute timer. Batch redeploys when several lands happen within 60 s. Wait for the health check to pass, then send a refresh event to open consoles.

before.title: Landing tool takes long build names, and auto-fixes and retries failed lands
before.detail: vps.build_land, build_start, build_stop and build_clean reject names over 40 characters (^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,39}$), but the orchestrator makes build IDs up to about 50 characters (e.g. demo-designer-finish-phase-2-s2-s3-resuming-from, skins-restyle-everything-badges-banner-and-every-visual-element). 1) In the axHub vps service, raise the name limit to match the orchestrator's longest IDs (at least 80), keeping the same safe character set. 2) If the orchestrator ever makes an ID the tools can't take, it shortens it consistently (folder, branch, tmux) instead of failing. 3) When build_land fails for any fixable reason (stray files, stale locks, name format), it fixes it and retries automatically, logging to the fix log. Real code clashes go to a conflict-fix build automatically. 4) Tests with long names. Repos: axHub (vps service config) and AmberX-AXF (orchestrator).

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 9 steps (1 Fable).

origin.said: Why, when it has a problem, when it gets rejected, aren't you just fixing it right away? I keep telling you over and over.

steps.text: Define the shared build-name contract used by both repos. Allowed names match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,79}$ (80 characters). Define one deterministic shortener: trim at a hyphen boundary, then append -<6-char hash of the full ID>, so the same long ID always maps to the same short name. The folder, branch and tmux session all use the short name. The orchestrator records long→short in its build record. Write the contract doc and the reference shortener module with its constants (max length, charset, hash length).
steps.why: Cross-port contract between the axHub vps service and the AmberX-AXF orchestrator

steps.text: axHub vps service: replace the hard-coded ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,39}$ in build_land, build_start, build_stop and build_clean with one shared constant from service config allowing up to 80 characters, with the same safe character set. Error messages state the limit and the offending length.

Orchestrator: route every place that makes a build ID, worktree folder, branch name or tmux session through build-name.mjs. When an ID exceeds the tools' limit, shorten it consistently instead of failing. Store long_id and short_id in the build record and journal. Lookups accept either form.
files: AmberX-AXF: apps/orchestrator/ (ID creation, worktree, branch, tmux spawn)

steps.text: Orchestrator: build_land failure classifier. Parse build_land errors into categories: stray_files (untracked or tmp files such as *.json.tmp-*), stale_lock (index.lock or a stale land lock with a dead PID), name_format (rejected name), code_conflict (real merge conflict) and unknown. Unit-testable pure function with fixtures from real failure output.

Orchestrator: auto-fix and retry loop around build_land. For each fixable category, apply the fixer: remove or commit stray tmp files after looking at them, clear stale locks only if the owning PID is dead, re-derive the short name for format rejects. Then retry, up to 3 attempts. Each attempt, fix and outcome is appended to the fix log. Land state (attempt, last error, fix applied) is readable through the existing console build API, MCP, CLI and voice status read.
files: AmberX-AXF: apps/console-web/ build status route/MCP/CLI land-state fields

steps.text: Orchestrator: on code_conflict, or when retries are used up on an unknown error, automatically queue a conflict-fix build. The queued build links to the parent build, the conflicting files and the failed land log. The parent build is marked waiting-on-fix in place of failed. Log it to the fix log.

axHub tests: build_land, build_start, build_stop and build_clean accept the 50 to 64 character real IDs (demo-designer-finish-phase-2-s2-s3-resuming-from, skins-restyle-everything-badges-banner-and-every-visual-element) and an exactly-80-character name. They reject 81 characters, uppercase, a leading hyphen, slashes and dots.

AmberX-AXF tests: the shortener is deterministic, stays within the limit, keeps the folder, branch and tmux names identical, and has no collisions across the existing shipped build IDs. The classifier fixtures pass. The auto-fix loop recovers from stray files, stale locks and name format errors and logs to the fix log. A code conflict queues a conflict-fix build. A full long-name start, land and clean path is checked end to end against a mock vps.

Run the full test suites in both repos. Write the report: what changed, the name contract, each auto-fix category, the API reach of land state (REST, MCP, CLI, voice) and the test results with before and after. Add the THREADS row. Open PRs in axHub and AmberX-AXF, cross-linked, axHub merged first.

before.title: Skin chunk previews, interactive demos, and an IDE-style studio with floating tab groups, side-by-side compare and live split editor
before.detail: Follows the skins-as-section-packages build; upgrade that and reuse existing pieces (the IDE layout and tab groups from walkthrough-player-ide-layout-setting-collapsibl, the Demonstration designer, and UI asset designer). 1) PREVIEW EVERYWHERE: every list and grid that shows skin chunks or assets gets a preview action (hover thumbnail plus a full preview pane). 2) INTERACTIVE DEMO: if a chunk can be demoed (behaviour, layouts, components), Demo opens a live sandbox where you can actually use it. Otherwise it shows a rendered preview of what it looks like. 3) COMPARE: open chunks side by side in any number of containers, docked or floating. 4) IDE STUDIO VIEW (optional view, not forced): floating and dockable tab groups, each holding any asset types, with a chunk info panel (name, category, source skin, tags, used-by). Drag tabs between groups, and drag chunks onto each other or into a pack template to build new skins and assets. 5) SPLIT TAB: any tab can split into editor plus live preview, with real-time updates while editing. 6) Layouts can be saved and restored. Full REST, MCP, CLI and voice control. Desktop and phone screenshots go to UI Review grouped by screen.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 16 steps (3 Fable).

origin.said: When you're looking at these lists and any of the grids of these chunks, you can preview one, or open a demo of it if it can be demoed, an interactive demonstration where you can actually use it, or at the very least a preview of what the chunk looks like. And the ability to view them side by side, multiple containers with tab groups, mix and match elements in multiple floating containers to compare side by side. An IDE-style thing with a bunch of floating tab groups with different types of assets in them, with the info on the chunk, and you can drag them to each other and build new things side by side. Each tab can be split with a preview and an editor so you can see changes in real time.

steps.text: Design the chunk preview and demo contract and the studio layout schema. Chunk manifest fields: demo capability (interactive kind: behaviour, layout or component; sandbox entry; rendered-preview fallback) and a thumbnail spec. Studio layout document: tab groups (docked or floating, position and size), tabs (asset ref, type, split state), compare containers, and named saved layouts. Add a migration that upgrades the existing IDE layout settings from walkthrough-player-ide-layout and the skin section-package manifests from skins-as-section-packages.
steps.why: Schema and migration design shared by the skins, demo and studio ports

steps.text: Extend the framework IDE layout engine taken from walkthrough-player-ide-layout. Tab groups become dockable or floating. Groups hold tabs of any asset type through a tab-type registry. Tabs can be dragged between groups and between docked and floating groups. Groups can be nested into compare containers. All of this is driven by the new layout document.
steps.why: Changes how the IDE-layout GUI works for every app that uses it

steps.text: Add the split-tab primitive and the live-update channel. Any tab can split into an editor pane and a preview pane. Edits flow to the preview in real time over a debounced change stream with the same contract for every asset type. Bad edits show an error overlay in the preview and keep the last good render.
steps.why: Engine internals and a cross-port editor/preview contract

steps.text: Add server-side preview rendering for skin chunks and UI assets: a cached thumbnail renderer and a full-preview render endpoint. Thumbnails are invalidated when a chunk changes. Reuse the UI asset designer renderer.

Add a preview action to every list and grid that shows skin chunks or assets: the skins section-package lists, pack grids, the UI asset designer library and the demonstration designer pickers. Hovering shows a thumbnail and Preview opens a full preview pane.

Add full API control for preview. Deep link console_open target skins/preview/<chunk>. Readable preview state. Actions preview.open, preview.close and preview.thumbnail. All of it reachable the same way through REST routes, MCP console actions and plugin commands, the CLI and AmberX voice intents.

Add the interactive demo. Demo opens a live sandbox for demoable chunks (behaviour, layouts, components) by reusing the Demonstration designer sandbox, so you can actually use the chunk. Chunks that cannot be demoed fall back to a rendered preview. The Demo action is added next to Preview in every list and grid.

Add full API control for demo. Deep link console_open skins/demo/<chunk>. Readable sandbox state (running, mode interactive or rendered). Actions demo.open, demo.reset and demo.close. All of it reachable through REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

Add the compare view. Open any number of chunks side by side in containers that can be docked or floating. Containers can mix asset types, and each container is a tab group from the extended layout engine.

Add the IDE studio as an optional view, off by default and switched on with a setting, not forced. It shows floating and dockable tab groups holding any asset types, plus a chunk info panel with name, category, source skin, tags and used-by. Used-by comes from a reverse-reference index built on the server.

Add drag-to-compose in the studio. Dropping a chunk onto another chunk, or into a pack template, creates a new skin or asset draft through the UI asset designer and the skins section-package builder, then opens the draft in a new tab.

Wire split tabs into the studio and compare views for every asset tab type. Each type gets an editor and a live preview that updates in real time over the live-preview channel, with a split toggle on every tab.

Add saving and restoring of layouts. Named studio and compare layouts can be saved, listed, restored, renamed and deleted. They are stored per profile and the last-used layout is restored automatically.

Add full API control for compare, the studio, split tabs, compose and layouts. Deep links: console_open skins/studio, skins/compare?chunks=… and skins/studio?layout=…. Readable state: groups, tabs, split state, info panel. Actions: open, close and move tabs; float and dock groups; split and unsplit; compose; layout save, restore and delete; the studio-view setting. All of it the same through REST, MCP (console actions and plugin commands, control@1 for tokens), the CLI and voice.
Capture desktop and phone screenshots of the list previews, demo sandbox, rendered fallback, compare, studio, info panel, split tab and layouts, and send them to UI Review grouped by screen.

Add tests for the schema migration, the layout engine (drag, float, dock), split live updates, the preview, demo, compose and layout routes, and REST/MCP/CLI/voice parity. Then write the report at _claude/builds/reports/skin-chunk-previews-interactive-demos-and-an-ide.md, add the THREADS row, and open the PR. The PR lists how each UI feature is reached through deep link, REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

Add the interactive demo. Demo opens a live sandbox for demoable chunks (behaviour, layouts, components) by reusing the Demonstration designer sandbox, so you can actually use the chunk. Run the suites and write _claude/builds/reports/standing-rule-in-every-brief-fix-problems-yourse.md. Add a THREADS.md row. Open a PR that states this build adds no UI and lists how the fix-log tool is reached (CLI / MCP / REST / voice).

before.title: Split builds pages (Build Manager = Pending + Complete; Orchestrator = Queued + Active) with one clean shared table design
before.detail:
Replaces one-builds-page-pending-queued-built-tabs-remove (mark superseded).

Pages: Build Manager owns Pending (create, edit, prioritize, Send to orchestrator) and Complete (finished builds sent back by the orchestrator: account that actually built it, model, cost, PR, land status). Build orchestrator owns only Queued and Active (route, assign account, hold, cancel/return to Pending); finished builds go back to Build Manager Complete. Remove every other builds table and the separate Build queue screen (redirect).

Design: one shared framework build-table asset used by all four tabs so they look the same. Each build is one clean compact line (title, priority, status badge, steps done/total, account, model) that expands; inside the expanded row, collapsible sections/sub-grids (steps with state, runs/sessions, cost, files/PR, Brett's words, log tail). Per-tab columns differ only where needed: Active shows a live elapsed timer, steps complete with a progress bar, current step, account actually running it; Queued shows position and why it's waiting; Complete shows duration, cost, who built it. Clean, minimal, theme tokens only, phone and desktop. Screenshots to UI Review. Full API/voice control.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 11 steps (2 Fable).

origin.said: Clean those tables up. One line that's expandable, with collapsible grids or sections inside the expanded row. All the tables need to look the same. The active ones need to show the timer, how long they've been going, how many steps are complete. Build manager will have pending and complete. Orchestrator will have active and queued.

steps.text: Define the build lifecycle contract between Build Manager and the orchestrator. Pending → Send → Queued. Queued → cancel/return → Pending. Queued → Active. Active → finished → Build Manager Complete. The completion record carries the account that actually built it, model, cost, PR, land status, start/end/duration and steps done/total. Add a store schema version bump plus a migration that moves existing finished, queued and active records into the new buckets. Mark one-builds-page-pending-queued-built-tabs-remove as superseded by this build.
steps.why: Schema + migration design and the cross-port handoff contract between two apps

steps.text: Create the shared framework build-table asset used by all four tabs. Each build is one compact line: title, priority, status badge, steps done/total, account, model. The line expands, and the expanded row holds collapsible sections and sub-grids. Use a per-tab column config so extra columns appear only where declared. Include an expand/collapse state API, theme tokens only, and a responsive phone/desktop layout.
steps.why: New shared framework GUI component that changes how build tables render across apps

steps.text: Add the build-table section renderers: steps with state, runs/sessions, cost, files/PR, Brett's words, and log tail. Add the live elements: an elapsed timer, a steps-complete progress bar and a current-step cell. Add the Queued position and 'why waiting' cells. Add the Complete duration, cost and built-by cells.
Rebuild the Build Manager Pending tab on the shared build-table, with create, edit, prioritize and Send to orchestrator. Remove the old Pending table markup.

Add the Build Manager Complete tab on the shared build-table. It shows finished builds sent back by the orchestrator: account that built it, model, cost, PR link, land status and duration. Expanded sections show steps, runs, cost, files/PR, Brett's words and log tail.

Give Build Manager full API control for Pending and Complete. Deep links: console_show/console_open targets build-manager/pending, build-manager/complete and build-manager/build/<id>, plus expanded state. State is readable through list/get. Actions: create, edit, prioritize, send-to-orchestrator, open/expand. Expose all of this through REST routes, MCP console actions/plugin commands, the CLI subcommands and AmberX voice intents, with the same behavior on all four.

Rebuild the orchestrator page with only Queued and Active tabs on the shared build-table. Queued shows position and why it's waiting, with route, assign account, hold, and cancel/return to Pending. Active shows the live elapsed timer, steps-complete progress bar, current step and the account actually running it. When a build finishes it is posted to Build Manager Complete through the handoff contract.

Give the orchestrator full API control for Queued and Active. Deep links: orchestrator/queued, orchestrator/active and orchestrator/build/<id>. State is readable: position, wait reason, elapsed, steps done/total, current step, account. Actions: route, assign account, hold/unhold, cancel/return to Pending. Expose all of this through REST, MCP (console actions, plugin commands, control@1 where tokens are involved), the CLI and AmberX voice, with the same behavior on all four.

Remove every other builds table and the separate Build queue screen. Old routes and deep links (build-queue, builds, built) redirect to the matching new tab in the REST, MCP, CLI and voice aliases. Delete dead CSS and JS.
Update the docs for the page split, the shared build-table asset and the API reach. Take phone and desktop screenshots of all four tabs, collapsed and expanded, and post them to UI Review.

Final step: tests, report, THREADS row and PR. Tests cover the build-table render, expand and sections, the store migration, the handoff Pending→Queued→Active→Complete and return-to-Pending, redirects, and REST/MCP/CLI/voice parity for every action. Run the suite. Write the report to _claude/builds/reports/split-builds-pages-build-manager-pending-complet-2.md and add a THREADS row. Open the PR, stating how each UI feature is reached through the deep link, state read, actions and settings via REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

before.title: Skin rule: overrides are local only; global changes only by applying a whole skin
before.detail: Amends the skins naming-contract build. Precedence: axHub base < skin (by canonical role) < per-screen skin < per-element override. An override changes only that element. Global changes are made ONLY by applying a whole skin; editing a button inside one plugin or app never propagates to other plugins/apps. Enforce in the inline editor (no 'apply everywhere' outside the skin editor) and document in CLAUDE.md rules.

before.title: Reserve build IDs at once: add returns the ID with the veto countdown
before.detail: Today pending_change add (and control_add on planner.builds/plans) is held on the 90 s veto countdown and the orchestrator only assigns the build ID when it runs, so callers (Claude sessions) must guess the ID from the title to add notes. Fix: the orchestrator (ID registry) reserves the ID the moment the call arrives, before the hold, and returns it in the held result (e.g. reservedId). Notes, sub prompts and status calls on a reserved ID queue up and apply in order once the add runs; if Brett denies the add, the reservation and anything queued on it are dropped. IDs never collide (registry check). Same for plan_park and plan_add. Tests: add returns the id while held; a note on the reserved id lands after the add; deny drops both.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.
Split by Claude into 8 steps (2 Fable).

origin.said: Why do you have to guess its ID? Why can't you get it? ... Yeah, of course.

steps.text: Design the reservation model in the orchestrator's ID registry. Add a `reserved` state with reservedAt, origin call, kind (build|plan) and holdId. Add a per-ID ordered queue of pending ops (note, sub prompt, status), each with a seq and a payload. Store it in _claude/builds/store.json and add a migration that leaves existing entries untouched. Write the registry API in pipeline-core.mjs: reserveId(title, kind) checks for collisions against live builds, plans, shipped and existing reservations; commitReservation(id) turns a reservation into a real build; dropReservation(id) removes it and its queue.
steps.why: Schema and migration design for the build ID registry, which every port's contract depends on

steps.text: Change the veto-hold contract so the ID is reserved before the hold starts. Held results carry reservedId, holdId and secondsLeft. On approve or timeout, commitReservation runs and then the queued ops are replayed in seq order. On deny, dropReservation runs. Write down the contract for every caller: pending_change add, control_add on planner.builds/plans, plan_park, plan_add.
steps.why: Cross-port contract change to the held-result shape that all callers rely on

steps.text: Wire pending_change add and control_add (planner.builds and planner.plans) through reserveId so the held result returns reservedId right away. Approve and deny on the hold call commit or drop the reservation.
Wire plan_park and plan_add the same way: reserve the ID before the hold, return reservedId in the held result, and commit or drop when the hold resolves.

Queue notes, sub prompts and status calls that target a reserved ID. The note, sub prompt and status handlers check whether the ID is reserved and, if so, add the op to the queue instead of failing. The queued result says queued:true with its seq. Replay applies the ops in order after the add runs.
Show the reserved ID and the queued op count on the veto countdown card in the console Build manager. Add a 'copy ID' action. Deep link: console_show target build-orchestrator/hold/<reservedId>.

API part for the reservation and countdown UI. REST: GET /api/builds/reservations and GET /api/builds/reservations/<id> read the state (status, secondsLeft, queued ops); POST approve and POST deny act on the hold. MCP: console actions builds.reservation.get, builds.reservation.approve and builds.reservation.deny, plus control@1 for planner items. CLI: axf builds reservation get|approve|deny <id>. AmberX voice intents for the same three actions. All four surfaces call the same handlers.

Tests, report and PR. Write tests for: add returns the ID while held; a note on the reserved ID lands after the add runs; deny drops the reservation and its queued note; no ID collision when two adds with the same title arrive together; plan_park and plan_add return reservedId; REST, MCP and CLI give the same results. Write _claude/builds/reports/reserve-build-ids-at-once-add-returns-the-id-wit.md. Add the THREADS row. Open the PR, stating how the reservation and countdown are reached through the deep link, REST, MCP, CLI and voice.

origin.said: In every plugin's appearance settings, as soon as you make a change off inherit from axHub there's a save button lit up. Save prompts a dialog with a default name with the date and type of change. Saved, the button goes grey. Every change makes a new save. steps.text: In every plugin's Appearance settings: 1) When inherit-from-axHub is off and there are unsaved changes, a Save button lights up; no changes = no Save button. Saved = Save turns grey and disabled until the next edit. 2) Save opens a dialog prefilled with a default name (date + type of change), editable. Each save stores a new per-plugin appearance asset (layout, style, behavior, colour etc. for that plugin only); every later change makes a new save. 3) Switching back to inherit from axHub keeps the custom state saved so it can be restored. 4) A Revert/Restore button opens a dialog listing all saves for that plugin with a side-by-side preview: what it will look like restored vs now. Full API/CLI control.

before.detail: Brett, Oct 30 2026 (voice): Grid of push batches with live badges, Merge/Hold on rows, expandable PR sub-grid, failing check + Fix. Dense: small type, small badges, no clutter. Left click opens review, right click menu. PR BROWSER (Brett, Oct 31): a tab listing every open PR across AmberX-AXF, axHub and Build-Pilot. One dense line per PR with everything: number, title, branch, built by (agent/session), live checks badge, behind main, mergeable/conflict, in which batch, age, cost. Expand a row: every check with its error lines, files changed, commits, description, linked build/plan, and actions: Fix, Merge (via batch), Add to batch, Close. Sort/search/filter like every grid; live updates. ROW LEAD (Brett): every row starts with the PR number + a plain-English line of what it does (e.g. '#187 Audio Extract: pulls audio out of screen recordings, no mic'), written from the actual diff not just the title; badges follow on the same line. SCREENSHOTS (Brett): every PR gets BEFORE (main) and AFTER (PR branch) screenshots of the screens it touches, captured automatically by CI/headless browser (web) and emulator (Android); small before/after thumbnails on the row, side-by-side or slider compare in the expanded view, stored with the PR. SCREENSHOT CORRECTION (Brett): do NOT build a new capture system - REUSE the existing pre-build and post-build screenshots the framework already takes (find them first). BEFORE = the existing pre-build screenshot. AFTER: if the PR/build is not done yet, show a PREDICTED screenshot (rendered mockup of the expected result from the build spec + diff so far, clearly badged 'Predicted'); as soon as the build finishes, the real post-build screenshot replaces it automatically (badge 'Real'), live, no refresh. FEATURE SHOTS (Brett): the existing pre/post-build screenshots are NOT enough - they must show the ACTUAL FEATURE the PR built. Per PR, build a feature map from the diff (changed plugins, components, routes, menus, dialogs -> the screens and states that show them). Drive the existing capture tooling to navigate to each one, open it (expand the row, open the dialog/menu, switch the tab, put it in the right state with demo data), and shoot it: BEFORE on main, AFTER on the PR branch. Each shot cropped to the feature plus a full-screen version, web + Android. Brand-new UI has no before: show a 'New' card. Every feature shot shows Predicted (mockup from spec + diff) until the build is done, then the real shot replaces it live. Captions say which feature each shot is. Missed features (no shot) flagged on the row.

origin.brief:
# Build: amberx-floating-toolbar-always-on-top-mic-approvals-build-status

## Brett said (verbatim)
> 

## Addendum 1 (Brett (voice))
> Actually, make AmberX notifications a widget. ... On any toolbar or any banner.

## What to build
Continue build "AmberX floating toolbar (always on top): mic + approvals + build status" (amberx-floating-toolbar-always-on-top-mic-approvals-build-status) [amberx] — Phase 1, model Opus.
What Brett asked for (build-origin@1, his words come first; a paraphrase never replaces them):
Addendum 1: "Actually, make AmberX notifications a widget. ... On any toolbar or any banner."
Model switches: a downgrade (e.g. Fable → Opus) is fine. Fable upgrades need no approval right now (Brett, Nov 4 2026: "If it needs Fable, set it to be Fable"): a step that needs Fable (schemas, asset types, contracts, engines/kernel, cross-app protocols) is set to Fable and runs on Fable; the switch is recorded on the build. Never launch a step on a higher model than it is pinned to: raise the step first.
Rules: stay in this one session; no sub-agents; steps ≤ 30 min; read only the files listed; stop at the end of this phase.
Look: UI code (handwritten or generated) conforms to the hot-swappable asset system: every colour, size, spacing, font, radius and border comes from asset tokens (--fx-* colour/style, --fx-type-* / --fx-dens-* / --fx-size-* scale, --fx-radius-*, --fx-border-w; Kotlin: Axf.colors / Axf.type / Axf.space / Axf.shapes), framework controls instead of raw ones, no var() fallbacks. `node framework/cli/check-theme.mjs` and `check-controls.mjs` must pass (CI fails otherwise); `node framework/cli/scale-adopt.mjs <path>` moves most literals onto the tokens.
API: Everything comes with an API (Brett, Nov 8 2026): anything this build adds or changes that has a UI gets full API control: a deep link that opens it (console_show / console_open target), its state readable, and every action and setting it offers callable without the UI, through the console API (REST), MCP tools (console actions, plugin commands, control@1 for tokens and planner items), the CLI and voice (AmberX), all four the same. A UI-only feature is not done; say in the PR how each one is reached.
Branch: claude/amberx-floating-toolbar-always-on-top-mic-approvals-build-status
Steps in this phase (4 left, ~2 h):
[ ] s1 (~30 min) Overlay permission + floating draggable bubble/toolbar service, always on top, snap/collapse
[ ] s2 (~30 min) Mic button wired to hands-free/talk listener; approvals badge with live count and approve/deny in place
[ ] s4 (~30 min) Make it a standard toolbar: same drop-on behaviour as every other toolbar (registered in Toolbars settings, plugins can register and drop items onto it, reorder/remove), so Brett's own plugins attach later
[ ] s3 (~30 min) Build status item, settings (items, size, opacity), token-styled assets; screenshots to UI Review
Tick each step: node apps/console-web/plugins/build-orchestrator/orchestrator.mjs act step amberx-floating-toolbar-always-on-top-mic-approvals-build-status <stepId> done — it reaches main at once (builds-live). Link your branch / PR: node framework/cli/builds-live.mjs link amberx-floating-toolbar-always-on-top-mic-approvals-build-status --branch <b> --pr <n>.
Watch live: when you start on a screen, run `node framework/cli/axf.mjs focus <app> [route] [css-selector] --note "…"` so the live preview follows you.
Screenshots that are not for approval (checking a screen, live captures, before/after): axf shot <file> --name "…" --app … --screen … --group "<build name>" (UI Review → Screenshots; ui-review-item@1), never the review queue.

before.detail: Every Shipped Features entry, build (Pending/Queued/Built) and Plan Studio plan that relates to a UI, screen, dialog, plugin or setting carries go-to hooks. The manifest records the UI targets it touched (view ids, dialogs, settings tabs/keys, plugin, element selectors) from the registry. In the row: an 'Open' button (opens the main target), and in the expanded row a 'Go to' list of every target. Clicking opens it in the console (or Molly/AmberX) via deep link / console_show, focused, scrolled into view, centered and highlighted. Works on desktop and phone; targets that no longer exist show as 'removed'. Backfill hooks for already shipped entries from their reports/plugin.json ui blocks. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control ('open what build X changed'). Tests: a hook opens the right view and highlights the element.

before.title: UI Roller: roll a random style on any UI element
before.detail: New UI Roller plugin (console, AmberX, Molly, axHub web; every app built on the framework). 1) Context menu on EVERY UI element (dialogs, windows, panels, bars, buttons, inputs, menus, text, widgets; all registry assets): 'Roll style' and, when the element has a roll, 'Reset element'. 2) 'Roll style' opens a dialog: checkboxes for what to roll (colours, typography, spacing/density, size, radius/shape, borders, shadows, motion, icons), optional scope (this element / all of its type / its plugin), live preview, Re-roll, Apply. Rolls stay within valid token ranges and keep contrast readable. Apply saves the result as asset token overrides (local-first, like other overrides). 3) Main Settings > Rolled assets page: lists every app and plugin with its rolled assets (tree, counts, filters, search); each shows a live preview of the asset and its roll; actions: Reset (one), Reset selected (multi-select), Reset all. Undo/history per roll. 4) Applying a skin, design pack or theme clears EVERY rolled asset: covered ones take the new look, all others go back to their defaults. 5) Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control and deep links for roll, reset, reset selected/all and the page. Stock framework controls; 3 layout options to UI Review; tests (roll writes tokens, reset restores, theme apply clears all rolls); report.

before.title: Shipped Features: live manifests from dispatch to done, badges + progress meter
before.detail: Builds on shipped-manifest-api (landed 79ed472c0f1f, shipped-manifest@1). Today the manifest is sent only when a build lands. Change: the orchestrator sends a manifest to Shipped Features (and Plan Studio, per the queued Plan Studio manifest build) at every event: when it dispatches the job, on every build update (model/account change, note, hold, guard stop), on every step completed, and on completion/land. Each manifest is versioned (sequence number, previous version kept as history) and validated. The Shipped Features entry exists from dispatch, not only after landing, and shows a live status badge (dispatched, building, step x/y, waiting on UI Review, held, stopped by guard, failed, landed, shipped) plus a progress meter (steps done / total, time and cost used vs estimate), updated in real time (live push, no refresh). History view per entry shows every manifest. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control and deep link. Tests: dispatch creates the entry, each step tick bumps the version and meter, land sets shipped; invalid manifest is refused with the reason.

notes.text: Brett: "it lists what files were touched too, but they're hidden... in a collapsible, in an expanded row... you gotta expand a few things to get to them. They'll open in a dialog, which also you can click the files and open in a read-only editor. Checkbox to make it editable." Each manifest lists the files touched (added/changed/deleted, per step). In Shipped Features they sit tucked away: entry row > expand > Details > collapsed 'Files touched' section (grouped by step and folder, counts). Clicking it opens a dialog with the file list; clicking a file opens it in a read-only code editor (syntax highlight, diff vs before toggle). A 'Make editable' checkbox in the editor switches it to edit mode; saving goes through a normal commit with Brett's name and a change entry, never silent. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control.
Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Brett: "when you open the file, it will jump to the feature that you found it through and highlight it. In focus, centered in screen." The manifest records, per touched file, the line ranges each step/feature changed. Opening a file from a Shipped Features entry scrolls the editor to that feature's code, centers it on screen, and highlights the changed lines (theme highlight colour); if a feature touched several spots, next/previous buttons jump between them. Same when opened via API/deep link (file + feature + range).

Brett: "Any failed, any errors that are file related get sent to the log with links to the file with the bad code there, the conflicted code, and highlighted and in focus." Every file-related failure (test/typecheck/lint/CI errors, merge conflicts, guard stops, parse errors in JSON) is written to the terminal log and the Shipped Features entry's manifest with file path + line range + message. Each log line carries a link; clicking it opens the file in the read-only editor scrolled to the bad or conflicted code, centered and highlighted (conflicts show both sides). Same via API/deep link.

Brett: "also make an errors column that's hideable. With a collapse button." In the Terminal plugin (console-terminal), add an Errors column: a side column next to the output showing only the file-related errors (file, line, message, build, time; click opens the file at the bad code, centered and highlighted). It has a collapse button (collapses to a thin strip with an error count badge) and can be hidden entirely from the Terminal toolbar/settings; state remembered. Filters by build, severity, plugin. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control.

Brett: prompt field to jump into a headless session. A running claude -p can't take input, so: a prompt field (on the build's Shipped Features entry, the Errors column line, and the session window) that, on send, does NOT send right away: it opens a confirm dialog warning that the running session will be stopped and any unfinished, uncommitted work in progress may be lost, showing what's at risk (current step, uncommitted files count, time/cost so far). Only on Confirm: stop the session cleanly (let it commit if it can), then resume the SAME session (claude --resume <session id>) with Brett's prompt so its context is kept; logged as a build note and a manifest update. Cancel keeps the prompt as a draft. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control, with the same confirm step.

before.title: Headless loop guards: stop endless loops and searches
before.detail: Guards on every headless session the orchestrator launches (claude-headless.sh + agent-slots + the running-builds watchdog's afterTick hook in pipeline.mjs): 1) Hard caps per session: --max-turns, wall time and cost cap derived from the step estimates (e.g. 2x estimate), settings with defaults. 2) Step progress timer: no step tick within 1.5x the step's estimate -> warn note, at 2x -> stop the session, build back to pending with the reason. 3) Loop detector reading the live log: the same command/tool call (or near-identical grep/find/sed) repeated N times, or M searches in a row with no edit/commit -> stop and note. 4) Search budget per step (e.g. 15 greps/finds) written into the brief and enforced by the detector. 5) Every stop: build note with the reason and last log lines, AmberX notification (normal notification, not an alarm), slot released, no auto-relaunch of a looped step until Brett says. 6) Brief line: 'If you can't find something in 3 searches, stop and leave a note.' Settings in orchestrator settings (categorized sections), full API/MCP/CLI/voice control. Tests with fake logs: repeated command, search spree, no tick, cost cap.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Brett: "I need a way to manage the safeguards." Add a Safeguards panel (orchestrator settings, its own section, also reachable from the build's row): turn each guard on/off; edit turns cap, time cap (x estimate), cost cap, no-tick warn/stop multipliers, repeat-command count, search budget; per-build and per-queue overrides; a live view of each running session against its limits (turns, time, cost, searches used); a log of every guard stop with the reason, last log lines and buttons: Relaunch, Raise limit and relaunch, Send back to pending. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control and a deep link. Stock controls, 3 layout options to UI Review.

Brett on managing the safeguards: "I don't want the file itself to be editable. I want it to be view. You can view the file with steps. Make it an MD file with bullet points for the rules. And create a sortable, collapsible tree with a whole shitload of different rules, of snippets. When you click it, it will pop a dialogue to let you add the custom fields that it requires for the snippet and it will insert it." Build: 1) The safeguards live as a Markdown rules file (one bullet per rule, grouped by heading), shown READ-ONLY in the panel (rendered view with the steps it applies to); no free-text editing. 2) A snippet library: a sortable, searchable, collapsible tree (category > sub-category > snippet) with a large set of ready rule snippets (turn caps, time/cost caps, no-tick timeouts, repeat-command and search-spree limits, file/folder fences, no sub-agents, model limits, test-before-commit, stop-and-note rules, etc.). 3) Clicking a snippet opens a dialog with the fields it needs (number, duration, $, path, model, scope: global/queue/build/step) with validation and a preview line; Insert adds the bullet to the rules file. 4) Each inserted rule can be toggled, moved, or removed from the panel (structured actions, still no raw edit); every change is versioned with history and undo. 5) The orchestrator and the loop detector read their limits from this file; the brief gets the bullets that apply to the step. Full API/MCP/CLI/voice control; stock controls; 3 layout options to UI Review.

Brett: "the dialogue that needs custom parameters for the rules, any that are like file names or specific things already have a list to choose from for the custom parameters." In the snippet fields dialog, every field whose values already exist is a pick list (searchable dropdown or tree picker), not free text: file and folder paths (from the repo tree / plugin registry), plugins, apps, builds, queues, steps, Claude accounts, API accounts, models, agents/crew, tools, commands, settings keys. Multi-select where a rule takes several. Free text only for true free values (numbers, durations, $ amounts) and those get validated inputs with units.

Brett: "There has to be filters too, where you put in for the list of certain types of parameters. There's got to be filters." Every pick list in the snippet dialog has filters fitting its type, plus search: files/folders by app, plugin, folder, file type/extension, changed recently, owned by a build; plugins by app, category, enabled; builds by status, queue, model, category, date; queues by account type; steps by build and state; accounts by role, model available, health; models by tier; agents by role/skill; tools by service; settings keys by plugin/section. Filters combine, show counts, can be cleared, and remember the last used per field.

Brett: "list of features. Stack. And the list of predefined search terms based on what the rule is." 1) Filters stack (combine) and include a 'feature' filter: pick from the Shipped features list / plugin feature catalog to narrow files, builds and steps to one feature. 2) Each snippet carries predefined search terms and preset filter stacks that fit that rule (e.g. a file-fence rule offers 'server routes', 'web views', 'plugin.json', 'tests', 'schemas'; a model rule offers 'Fable-only steps', 'UI steps'), shown as quick chips in the pick list; tap one to apply. Brett can save his own presets per snippet.

Brett: "as you type in the field, it automatically drops down the list of all the ones that match. Whatever you type. In real time. Letter per letter." Every parameter field is a type-ahead combobox: the match list drops down on the first letter and updates on every keystroke (fuzzy match, matched letters highlighted, within the active filters), keyboard up/down/enter and tap to pick. Fast on large lists (indexed/virtualized, no lag).

Brett: "And they pop up in a categorized tree." The live type-ahead drop-down shows its matches as a categorized collapsible tree (e.g. app > plugin > folder > file; queue > build > step; account type > account), branches with matches auto-expand, counts per branch, empty branches hidden; picking a branch can select all under it where the rule allows several.

steps.text: Guards on every headless session the orchestrator launches (claude-headless.sh + agent-slots + the running-builds watchdog's afterTick hook in pipeline.mjs): 1) Hard caps per session: --max-turns, wall time and cost cap derived from the step estimates (e.g. 2x estimate), settings with defaults. 2) Step progress timer: no step tick within 1.5x the step's estimate -> warn note, at 2x -> stop the session, build back to pending with the reason. 3) Loop detector reading the live log: the same command/tool call (or near-identical grep/find/sed) repeated N times, or M searches in a row with no edit/commit -> stop and note. 4) Search budget per step (e.g. 15 greps/finds) written into the brief and enforced by the detector. 5) Every stop: build note with the reason and last log lines, AmberX notification (normal notification, not an alarm), slot released, no auto-relaunch of a looped step until Brett says. 6) Brief line: 'If you can't find something in 3 searches, stop and leave a note.' Settings in orchestrator settings (categorized sections), full API/MCP/CLI/voice control. Tests with fake logs: repeated command, search spree, no tick, cost cap.

before.title: Agent profile schema: skills + personas, with a big template library
before.detail: Contract work (Fable). New asset schemas for crew agents: agent-skill@1 (name, domain, what it does, tools allowed, files/areas it owns, rules, checks it runs, model preference, cost cap, examples) and agent-persona@1 (name, nickname, voice/tone, job title, avatar, how it reports, strengths, limits), plus agent-profile@1 that combines one persona with several skills. Validators, fixtures, CI check. Ship a large library of boilerplate templates: skills (React UI, Kotlin/Compose, Python server, plugin manifests, themes/skins, tests, docs, merge-fixer, CI fixer, slot watchdog, account health, notifications, voice/API wiring, security review, UI Review designer, demo/pitch writer, data/Postgres, deploy/Coolify, refactor, perf) and personas (lander, reviewer, builder, watchdog, reporter, etc.). Template picker + 'new from template' in the Crew plugin; migrate the existing roster (Earl, Rhonda, Sully, Lenny, Gina, Paulie, Joey, Vinnie) onto it. Orchestrator reads skills when assigning steps. Every UI gets full API + voice + MCP/CLI control. Settings in categorized collapsible sections; 3 UI options to UI Review; tests; report.

notes.text: Split by rules (Claude: claude exit 1: Error: Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print): one step per line of the request, review the steps.

Brett additions: (1) HUNDREDS of pre-made skills and dozens and dozens of agent templates, not ~20. (2) Skills sortable/filterable by agent type (builder, reviewer, lander, watchdog, designer, writer, data, ops, etc.), plus search and tags. (3) Drag-and-drop agent designer: drag skills, tools and a persona onto an agent card to build it. (4) ONE new Agent Manager interface that merges and REPLACES the existing agent/crew screens (skills, tools, personas, roster); remove the old UI (keep code for harvesting). Clean, nice design. (5) Include a RAG database: agents get a retrieval knowledge base (index docs/code/memory, embeddings, search) with RAG skills; manageable in the Agent Manager. # Build: amberx-build-notifications-for-every-stage-start

At: 2026-11-10T20:56:54.475Z
> I'll get a notification every time a build starts, completes, ready for merge, and goes live, right?

## What to build
Continue build "AmberX build notifications for every stage: start, complete, ready to merge, merged, live" (amberx-build-notifications-for-every-stage-start) — Phase 1, model Opus.
What Brett asked for (build-origin@1, his words come first; a paraphrase never replaces them):
Brett said (2026-11-10 20:56):
"I'll get a notification every time a build starts, completes, ready for merge, and goes live, right?"
Model switches: a downgrade (e.g. Fable → Opus) is fine. Fable upgrades need no approval right now (Brett, Nov 4 2026: "If it needs Fable, set it to be Fable"): a step that needs Fable (schemas, asset types, contracts, engines/kernel, cross-app protocols) is set to Fable and runs on Fable; the switch is recorded on the build. Never launch a step on a higher model than it is pinned to: raise the step first.
Rules: stay in this one session; no sub-agents; steps ≤ 30 min; read only the files listed; stop at the end of this phase.
Look: UI code (handwritten or generated) conforms to the hot-swappable asset system: every colour, size, spacing, font, radius and border comes from asset tokens (--fx-* colour/style, --fx-type-* / --fx-dens-* / --fx-size-* scale, --fx-radius-*, --fx-border-w; Kotlin: Axf.colors / Axf.type / Axf.space / Axf.shapes), framework controls instead of raw ones, no var() fallbacks. `node framework/cli/check-theme.mjs` and `check-controls.mjs` must pass (CI fails otherwise); `node framework/cli/scale-adopt.mjs <path>` moves most literals onto the tokens.
API: Everything comes with an API (Brett, Nov 8 2026): anything this build adds or changes that has a UI gets full API control: a deep link that opens it (console_show / console_open target), its state readable, and every action and setting it offers callable without the UI, through the console API (REST), MCP tools (console actions, plugin commands, control@1 for tokens and planner items), the CLI and voice (AmberX), all four the same. A UI-only feature is not done; say in the PR how each one is reached.
Steps in this phase (3 left, ~1.3 h):

Tick each step: node apps/console-web/plugins/build-orchestrator/orchestrator.mjs act step amberx-build-notifications-for-every-stage-start <stepId> done — it reaches main at once (builds-live). Link your branch / PR: node framework/cli/builds-live.mjs link amberx-build-notifications-for-every-stage-start --branch <b> --pr <n>.
Watch live: when you start on a screen, run `node framework/cli/axf.mjs focus <app> [route] [css-selector] --note "…"` so the live preview follows you.
Screenshots that are not for approval (checking a screen, live captures, before/after): axf shot <file> --name "…" --app … --screen … --group "<build name>" (UI Review → Screenshots; ui-review-item@1), never the review queue.

before.detail: Plain-code watchdog (zero tokens) on the headless build slots and queue: every ~30 s checks each running slot against reality (tmux alive, claude pid alive, log advancing); dead / finished / hung -> release slot, mark build failed with reason (auth, limit, crash, hung), tell the orchestrator, notify Brett (type slot). origin.said:
Assign a crew member (agent profile in the roster, e.g. a 'Slot Warden') whose only job is watching the headless build slots and queue, all the time, in plain code (zero tokens).

1. Every ~30 s: check each running slot in framework/cli/agent-slots.mjs against reality (tmux session alive, claude -p pid alive, log advancing). Today 3 builds died in 1-3 s on bad logins but kept all 3 slots, freezing the queue.
2. Dead / finished / hung (no log progress past a threshold) -> release the slot, mark the build failed with the reason (auth, limit, crash, hung), tell the orchestrator so it can relaunch/fail over (account-health-failover build), and notify Brett's phone (AmberX notification panel, type 'slot').
3. Report: a live slot/queue status the console and AmberX show; a log of every intervention.
4. Also fix the root: claude-headless.sh must always finish/release its slot when Claude exits, even on instant auth failure.

Duplicate guard (Brett): The watchdog and the launcher refuse or stop duplicate builds: same brief/goal running twice (e.g. memory-manager-r2 and -r3 both ran). On launch, compare against running + queued builds (name stem, brief source, build id); keep the furthest-along one, stop/dequeue the other, tell the orchestrator and notify Brett. Reuse the unlanded orchestrator-dup-check branch.

Per area: `node framework/cli/ui-parity.mjs gaps <area>`, then map each view/dialog in its plugin.json `ui` block (open = deep link, state = read command or value:<key>, actions = commands / console actions / settings, uiOnly with why), add any op that is missing, and `ui-parity.mjs write-baseline` once it went down. origin.said:
Standing rule: anything with a UI must have API functions that can do everything the UI can (open, read state, every action, every setting). Voice control is the app's main selling point and rides on this.

1. Orchestrator: every brief it writes for a build that touches UI includes this requirement explicitly (brief template + brief writer). Keep it short.
2. CI check: every registered UI asset/control/plugin view maps to API operations covering its actions and settings; fail when missing; report gaps.
3. Audit: list every existing UI lacking full API coverage, starting with the glossary/index Demonstration Designer and Book Builder; fix those two here, add the rest as pending builds.
4. Deep link per plugin view (URL that opens it) so agents can open any UI on the phone.

origin.said:
Standing rule: anything with a UI must have API functions that can do everything the UI can (open, read state, every action, every setting). Voice control is the app's main selling point and rides on this.

1. Orchestrator: every brief it writes for a build that touches UI includes this requirement explicitly (brief template + brief writer). Keep it short.
2. CI check: every registered UI asset/control/plugin view maps to API operations covering its actions and settings; fail when missing; report gaps.
3. Audit: list every existing UI lacking full API coverage, starting with the glossary/index Demonstration Designer and Book Builder; fix those two here, add the rest as pending builds.
4. Deep link per plugin view (URL that opens it) so agents can open any UI on the phone.

before.title: UI = API parity: framework React layer and libs (controls every app uses)
before.detail: Part of the "every UI is fully API-controllable" rule (ui-api@1; build ui-api-parity-rule, which did the Demonstration Designer and Book Builder and the CI check). 335 gaps across 1 UI area(s) today (framework/spec/ui-parity-baseline.json). Per area: `node framework/cli/ui-parity.mjs gaps <area>`, then map each view/dialog in its plugin.json `ui` block (open = deep link, state = read command or value:<key>, actions = commands / console actions / settings, uiOnly with why), add any op that is missing, and `ui-parity.mjs write-baseline` once it went down. Model of a full map: apps/console-web/plugins/glossary-index/plugin.json `ui`. Audit: _claude/builds/reports/ui-api-parity-rule/audit.md.

origin.said:
Standing rule: anything with a UI must have API functions that can do everything the UI can (open, read state, every action, every setting). Voice control is the app's main selling point and rides on this.

1. Orchestrator: every brief it writes for a build that touches UI includes this requirement explicitly (brief template + brief writer). Keep it short.
2. CI check: every registered UI asset/control/plugin view maps to API operations covering its actions and settings; fail when missing; report gaps.
3. Audit: list every existing UI lacking full API coverage, starting with the glossary/index Demonstration Designer and Book Builder; fix those two here, add the rest as pending builds.
4. Deep link per plugin view (URL that opens it) so agents can open any UI on the phone.

origin.said:
"We need a plugin that will let AmberX open up any website I tell her to."
(Context: amberx.open_url refused www.hostinger.com: "open_url only opens Brett's own sites (amberxai.com)".)

1. amberx.open_url (axHub device service) opens any http/https URL on Brett's paired phone, not only amberxai.com. Block non-http(s) schemes (intent:, file:, javascript:). Audit-log every open.
2. Setting in axHub (owner-only): mode = own sites only / allowlist / any site (default: any site, per Brett). Allowlist editable.
3. AmberX app: opens external sites in the phone's default browser; own sites keep opening in AmberX.
4. Tests, docs (decisions), PR to the merge queue. Do NOT land directly. If the AmberX APK needs a change, note it for an AmberX-AXF follow-up.

One session, lean chain.

origin.said:
"It's gonna be linked to our Gmail through axHub's MCP server, not Claude's. axHub is gonna connect to my Gmail, my Google Calendar, my Google Sheets. axHub needs to connect to my whole Google ecosystem."

1. Google service(s) in axHub: one OAuth sign-in (Brett clicks Connect in axHub web; tokens in the vault, refresh saved on every use). Scopes: Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, Drive, Contacts, Tasks (enable per service).
2. MCP tools per service (gmail.search/read/send/draft/label, calendar.list/create/update/delete/freebusy, sheets.read/write/append, drive.search/read/upload, contacts, tasks). Policies: reads allow; send email, delete, and calendar invites to others = confirm; other writes veto.
3. Events/webhooks (Gmail push, Calendar watch) published on axHub so the console can sync.
4. Docs (decisions), tests with a fake Google, PR to the merge queue. Do NOT land directly. Brett signs in after deploy.

One session, lean chain.

before.title: Molly gap: Expenses allows Molly's origin on /api/expenses/v1/* (CORS with credentials) so native screens read the ledger
before.detail: Found by molly-sign-in-once s1. From https://molly.amberxai.com, GET https://expenses.amberxai.com/api/expenses/v1/entries?limit=1 answers 401 with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin and the preflight answers 204 with no CORS headers, so a browser on Molly cannot call the ledger API with the axs_session cookie. The route handler (apps/expenses/app/api/expenses/v1/[...path]/route.ts, or proxy.ts) should answer an allow-list of amberxai.com app origins with Access-Control-Allow-Origin echoing the origin, Allow-Credentials true, Allow-Headers content-type, accept, authorization, x-expenses-user, Allow-Methods GET POST PATCH OPTIONS, Vary Origin, and an OPTIONS handler. Molly side is in place: apps/molly/src/molly/credentials.ts (expenses provider: cookie session or bearer token + X-Expenses-User).

## Brett said (verbatim)
At: 2026-11-10T21:38:57.321Z
> You might as well just build it over again and make it sick. Make it better. It's gotta be a full-blown Claude interface where I can either talk to Claude or talk to my Ollama. The Gizmo plugin is trash, the chat is trash, it used to be way better.

## What to build
Continue build "Rebuild Gizmo from scratch: full Claude-style chat interface, switch between Claude and local Ollama/Llama" (rebuild-gizmo-from-scratch-full-claude-style-cha) — Phase 1, model Opus.
What Brett asked for (build-origin@1, his words come first; a paraphrase never replaces them):
Brett said (2026-11-10 21:38):
"You might as well just build it over again and make it sick. Make it better. It's gotta be a full-blown Claude interface where I can either talk to Claude or talk to my Ollama. The Gizmo plugin is trash, the chat is trash, it used to be way better."
Model switches: a downgrade (e.g. Fable → Opus) is fine. Fable upgrades need no approval right now (Brett, Nov 4 2026: "If it needs Fable, set it to be Fable"): a step that needs Fable (schemas, asset types, contracts, engines/kernel, cross-app protocols) is set to Fable and runs on Fable; the switch is recorded on the build. Never launch a step on a higher model than it is pinned to: raise the step first.
Rules: stay in this one session; no sub-agents; steps ≤ 30 min; read only the files listed; stop at the end of this phase.
Look: UI code (handwritten or generated) conforms to the hot-swappable asset system: every colour, size, spacing, font, radius and border comes from asset tokens (--fx-* colour/style, --fx-type-* / --fx-dens-* / --fx-size-* scale, --fx-radius-*, --fx-border-w; Kotlin: Axf.colors / Axf.type / Axf.space / Axf.shapes), framework controls instead of raw ones, no var() fallbacks. `node framework/cli/check-theme.mjs` and `check-controls.mjs` must pass (CI fails otherwise); `node framework/cli/scale-adopt.mjs <path>` moves most literals onto the tokens.
API: Everything comes with an API (Brett, Nov 8 2026): anything this build adds or changes that has a UI gets full API control: a deep link that opens it (console_show / console_open target), its state readable, and every action and setting it offers callable without the UI, through the console API (REST), MCP tools (console actions, plugin commands, control@1 for tokens and planner items), the CLI and voice (AmberX), all four the same. A UI-only feature is not done; say in the PR how each one is reached.
Branch: claude/rebuild-gizmo-from-scratch-full-claude-style-cha

[ ] s1 (~30 min) Replace the current Gizmo chat. Full Claude.ai-quality interface: conversation list, streaming replies, markdown/code, attachments, voice talk mode, history search. Model switcher per chat: Claude (accounts/API) or local Ollama (amberx-llama container, Mistral Small 24B default, 7B option) via the internal API. Works in AmberX app, AmberX web app and console, with a real deep link. Keep what worked before the Nov 7 Fable rebuild.
[ ] s2 (~30 min) You might as well just build it over again and make it sick. Make it better. It's gotta be a full-blown Claude interface where I can either talk to Claude or talk to my Ollama. The Gizmo plugin is trash, the chat is trash, it used to be way better.
[ ] s3 (~20 min) Tests green, report _claude/builds/reports/rebuild-gizmo-from-scratch-full-claude-style-cha.md, THREADS row, commit, push, PR
